She answers her questions about the negotiations with Poss. She has had the sad news that in the dispute with Don Ricchini she will have to testify under oath. She has written to Don Accinelli that she wants to appeal; Vincenza is to tell her uncle so that he will take it up. Advice on the house and on moving a Sister.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I've just received your letter and reply at once to tell you what you want: the small reckoning you made for Poss seems too little to me, especially the Sunday one. Listen, you can do this: one Sunday buy everything [for] (le) our girls, who are 50, and you'll see much more is needed, because for a hundred girls you need at least 4 kg of mutton, and I don't think even that's enough. The daily figure seems too little to me too; I'll work it out now and then you'll take it to him.1

2. You did well about Sr. A. Cecilia; keep her with you and send Sr. A. Apollonia with the postulant, and clothe the other; I hope [Sr. A. Cherubina's trouble] is nothing much, so she can stay at Cortemaggiore too.2

3. Listen, Poss is right about the frontal (pagliolo) he speaks of: it's the one in the [loom room]; you know, that half-made altar where they used to put the cotton; understand? Try to send it to him at once; or rather, tell him to come and fetch it. Whatever will Poss have said? enough, send it at once; as for the rest, you did well.3

4. Forward with courage, for it is a time of great trial, truly on every side, my dear daughter; you know, we've lost the lawsuit and they've admitted all the oaths; I've written to Don Accinelli that I want to appeal; meanwhile you write the same to your uncle and ask him to take it up;4 you can understand: I've swallowed this pill without even a drop of water, for I must stifle everything inside me, being alone and having to keep silent about everything. Patience!

5. I don't know; you tell me the builder's bill is among the accounts; how is that? it must be for the few jobs he's done now, because I had paid the old one. Oh, when I hear you've paid them all it will be a real consolation. How it pains me! Tell me how much is still owing and whether you paid the merchant with the 500 F.5 You'll have called in the women to do the washing, won't you?

6. My dear, if only you could put the house in order a little and fill it with postulants! Accept the one you mentioned, provided she's strong; see whether you can send the sick girl to the Morte. And if you make Sr. A. Cecilia sacristan and wardrobe keeper, then you can send Sr. A. Geronima to the Morte or to S. P. d'Arena, for I'm always worried she's scheming with the Vice; you know what a tongue she has.6

7. So for the girls, you decide; try it out on a feast day and then you'll see better, and do the same for the daily cost; if your reckoning works out, write and tell me; for the rest, be assured I never told Mr Poss that 34 cents is enough for the girls. It isn't true; you know he says what he likes, bless him.

Goodbye, in haste,

your M. R.

1 Regarding the small reckoning. Finding inadequate the sum Emilio

Poss had set for the keep of the working girls in his establishment, Sr. A. Vincenza had objected. At his invitation she had calculated, item by item, the cost of each of our resident girls.

Before presenting him the account she had submitted it to the Mother, who gives suitable suggestions and even says she will work out the cost herself.

2 Sr. A. Cecilia is to stay in Piacenza in charge of the wardrobe; Sr. A. Apollonia is to go with the postulant to Sampierdarena; she is to clothe the other postulant.

As for Sr. A. Cherubina, she thinks she will soon recover and be able to go to Cortemaggiore.

3 The pagliolo: palliotto, the liturgical hanging covering the front of the altar; she had promised it to Poss. She now explains to Sr. A. Vincenza where to find it and urges her to deliver it promptly.

4 ...you know, we've lost the lawsuit: the Ricchini case; cf. letter of Accinelli

11.3.1874: "an appeal will be lodged and we'll see about doing all we can; but at that time, perhaps in three months, it would be good for you to send Sr. A. Vincenza to Genoa, but we'll talk about that further". Write to your uncle, the advocate Domenico Boccardo.

5 "...you tell me that among the accounts". Many debts still to be paid: carpenter, builder, whitewasher, gilder, miller, etc. "If only St Joseph would send me money to clear them all!"

6 Accept her: she is a postulant "without a cent, a peasant". Send to the Morte: to the infirmary of the second house in Piacenza. I'm worried.

Sr. A. Geronima talked too much and out of turn. The Mother fears she may be scheming with Sr. A. Carmelita, the Vice-Superior.

7 She repeats paragraph 1 and concludes that she should settle the matter with Poss.

Yes, she is to please her mother and write to her brother, kindly urging him to be good and console their mother. The Mother is still waiting for two more Sisters, already prepared, to be called. Cheer up, the Lord loves her; she must try to respond by keeping the rules and having the Sisters keep them.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I didn't answer you at once because I'm very busy and haven't even my secretary, who has gone to Piacenza. You tell me Mamma wants you to write to your brother; yes, my dear, please mamma, since it's such a small thing, and don't mind that your brother has never written to you. My dear, we must teach lay people humility and docility; so try to do it, with kind manners full of divine unction, and exhort him to remain a good Christian and be the consolation of your good Mamma.1

2. I hope that in the Sisters you will call — I long for it, so you can keep the observance better — so let me know soon that I should send them, and I'll send you a good cook, sensible and very observant, whom you'll like.2

3. Give my warm regards to the religious, and if you see the Bishop return his greetings and tell him I long to be at his feet to receive his holy blessing.3

4. Be cheerful; don't you see how much the Lord loves you? Try to respond by keeping your Rules and having your Sisters keep them, those whom God has entrusted [to you]; and you must see that they are always after his Heart: good, docile and observant. That is what it takes to please the Heart of God. Courage, my dear; remember that this mother of yours always holds you to the Heart of Jesus, so as one day to see you his perfect daughter.

Your affectionate MADRE R. G.

1 Sr. A. Carlotta did not intend to write to her brother: "I don't much feel like writing to him, because he has been too cruel to me and has not written to me even once".

2 For the two Sisters she wanted. Cf. 138,4.

3 The Mother had never been to Pennabilli. She was awaited by her Daughters, the

Bishop and all who loved the Sisters and valued their work.

If help is needed, she is to have some Sisters and postulants from the Sampierdarena house come to her during the day. She is to write to the Superior of S. Lazzaro so that Fr Defilippi may give the spiritual exercises to the Genoa communities. Carlotta would like to wear half-mourning, but she should first find out what is being done for the other granddaughters.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Today I received yours asking me again about the wardrobe keeper. I've already written to you about it once; perhaps you didn't get it? I told you to put Sr. A. Elisabetta, as she seems much better to me. For charity's sake, if you have work to do, do this: have some nuns and postulants sent from the house during the day and send them back in the evening.

2. And I warn you not on any account to let them take Sr. A. del Salvatore away from Sestri; if they want someone in Genoa for the begging round, let the Superior go, for she's strong and can very well do it.1 Sr. A. Vincenza writes that she is keeping Sr. A. Cecilia with her; you can take another, and then, once the postulants are clothed soon, you'll have nuns everywhere.

3. I want you to write to the Superior of S. Lazzaro to let Mr Defilippi come and give a short Retreat, both for S. P. d'Arena and for Genoa and, if possible, for you and for Sestri. While he's there keep him, so as to save looking for another.2

4. Be careful, my dear: when you receive my letters, read them properly, otherwise you make me repeat things many times. You can imagine I'm alone at the desk and have to deal with everything.

5. Listen, Carlotta keeps after me to write to you that she'd like a half-mourning dress; but first find out how long Mary and the others are made to wear full mourning, for I wouldn't want her to leave it off sooner. You can find out from Alessandro, so I'll know what to do. Then send her the samples first, because she wasn't happy with the one they made her here; she longs to take it off.3

6. So many things, my dear, on every side! Then I'd like you to try to make the contract4 and see how they intend to arrange everything; it's the Secretary who does it all anyway — he only has to draw it up, and it's all done. Greet all the Sisters for me, and believe me

your affectionate MADRE. God bless you all, and you in particular.

1 don't let them take: don't allow Sr. A. del Salvatore Orsi to be moved from Sestri.

Don Accinelli had opposed moving Sr.

A. Teresa from Genoa, because she did the begging round. (Cf. letter of Accinelli to M. Rosa

27.2.74); let the Superior go: Sr. A. Santina Solenghi.

2 Cf. L 206,9 and the relevant note. After the Exercises he could wait a little and preach them to the Sisters at Sestri too.

3 Carlotta... half-mourning. Her grandfather Francesco had died on 27 January last. Alessandro is to find out how long Mary (Giustina's daughter) and the other cousins are wearing mourning. You'll send fabric samples. She doesn't like the mourning dress made for her in Rome and longs to leave off mourning.

4 There was still no proper written contract.

She gives suitable advice and approves what she has done. She is to write to the Parish Priest of Bramaiano to send the girls; those of the Parish Priest of the Paganina are also to be accepted. She is to ask the Father to acknowledge the Mother's letters. She is to speak plainly to Don Biale about paying what he owes.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I've just received yours and answer what you want. I hear you have another 200 F.; so that makes 750 F. — seven hundred and fifty — pay the bills, for charity's sake.1

2. You do well not to send any to S. P. d'Arena; I'm sorry you had the washing done by the postulants, especially the one from Bramaiano; it's better to take on two women, so that the religious — I mean the postulants — don't (si) suffer.

3. I hear about the wine the Parish Priest sent; tell them not to drink it;2 yes, send all the sick to the Morte; that's my wish; and as soon as you can move the other one, do so. Leave at Poss the one that person put there; I think it's very good; so Sr. A. Veronica is to stay at Poss, being just right to be downstairs watching over the girls; and the one Francesca sends you, put her at Poss too.3

4. Listen, I think they've already sent them from Genoa; you should write to the Parish Priest of Bramaiano, who has a good number ready; so write to him at once if you need them.4

5. I hope you've received my letter about your uncle; for the rest I approve everything; all is well.5 Yes, the postulants who come to you, accept them all, provided they are strong and truly called.6 Take care of yourself in the cold; I'm eager for you to tell me you've paid the bills and how much is still owing. Don't overtire yourself; look after yourself.

6. Here everything is as usual, Trastevere the same; for the girls' aprons you can take the underskirts as you say; try, if you can, to see that the postulants have their bed and trousseau. I urge you not to cut linen cloth but to keep plenty.

7. So today you'll make the contract; blessed be God for it; I can't wait for the Sisters to be there.7 I hope all will go well and St Joseph won't always be beating us.8 I'm fairly well; give my regards to that person; for charity's sake tell him to acknowledge all my letters, for I always fear some may get lost.

8. There are also those of the Parish Priest of the Paganina, who are to be taken; see that he gives you something towards their uniform.9 Keep after Don Biale, because it's becoming serious; it's gone beyond a joke; what does he think? See whether he has none; I can't keep him. Try to make him understand; meanwhile they're laughing behind our backs. The expense is too great; I can't bear it any longer.10

Yours for an eternity, affectionate M. R.

1 I receive yours: of 9 March, and she answers point by point. A postulant has entered and brought F. 200.

2 The Parish Priest of Nizza, Don Ludovico Bixio, had sent "a large barrel of wine" ordered by the Mother.

3 Sr. A. Vincenza took the girl Teresina to the infirmary, and the next day will take Sr. A. Cherubina. She thinks Sr. A. Elvira well suited, as Fr Tornatore advised, to supervise the non-resident girls of the Poss factory.

4 I think Genoa has already sent the girls for the Poss factory. Write also to the Parish Priest of Bramaiano (Bettola). Cf. L 190, n. 7.

5 Cf. L 216,4.

6 Sr. A. Vincenza thought they should not be sent to Sampierdarena but kept in Piacenza.

7 The contract for Maddalena Parmigiani's house.

8 St Joseph won't always be beating us: he won't punish us by depriving us of providence.

9 those of the Parish Priest: the girls Don Elia Magnani was putting forward to be taken on as workers at the Poss factory.

10 Keep after... Don Biale was not paying what had been agreed, so that he was a burden on the Mother House's finances.

The debts are still not paid off. She is to pray to St Joseph to provide. Anna will not be clothed on the 25th. She is to put everything well in order. She may return to Rome after Easter with Don Accinelli. She is to be at peace: though far apart they are close; the Mother writes to her every day.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I've just received your letter enclosing the account of what is owed; I really hope Saint Anne and St Joseph will send it to you; it's too much on my mind.1 Blessed be God in his creatures; you've done everything well; I also approve your having the washing done by the postulants, so no one will know anything; you see, I was speaking of the one who belongs to the Parish Priest; enough, you've done everything well.2

2. Before laying in provisions, try to pay the bills, and then do it.

3. As you'll know, Anna won't be clothed on Lady Day; there are a thousand obstacles already; ask that person to write to her. What is he doing, sleeping? It seems impossible that it should take so long to answer.3

4. You did well to accept postulants; accept many; I've just received a letter from Cortemaggiore: Sr. A. Elvira must be removed quickly, and two would be needed; so clothe two and then send them. Remove Sr. A. Elvira and send her to S. P. d'Arena as you said. How dreadful, she really is undisciplined!

5. I'm answering the Superior Tommasina, for she asks whether they may assist women in childbirth; I say absolutely not; operations are one thing, this is another.

6. For your guidance, note that the builder's bill of 102.54 is paid, because I gave the money to Sr. A. Francesca to settle it beforehand; check it, say so. You also did well to send Sr. A. Geronima to the Morte, for I'd be sorry if she stayed at the house again, and let's not think any more of sending her anywhere; let her stay at the Morte;4 and so you can give the keys of the religious' wardrobe,5 and of those you know where the blankets were, where Superior Francesca put some linen, so they won't have to open the others, which I want kept always locked; she can also look after the sacristy and keep the guest quarters in good order, and you'll make her mistress of postulants; tell her to teach them [to] be very clean and to make them punctual at prayers and, in short, keep the timetable.

7. If this reaches you in time, send only Sr. A. Apollonia and Sr. A. Elvira to S. P. d'Arena, no more postulants; keep them all there. My dear, that S... at Trastevere is a goose and it's impossible to leave her there; for charity's sake find one with some sense; this one understands nothing.6

8. Make a triduum to St Joseph to send it all; how it rots my blood! I'm really waiting for you to come; you'd better stay until Don Accinelli passes through, as I've already written that you'll come with him the week after Easter, so you can put things in good order; patience is needed!7

9. My dear, see how we are always together; I write to you every day; you must have letters from me every day; I'm always in credit. So courage, for one day we shall never again have to be parted, for all eternity; yes, my God, you will give me my firstborn daughter closest to me of all. You tell me nothing about your health.8

10. I hope you've seen what they've done with the pork; see they don't lay hands on it and that it's well kept; and don't forget to get the piglets from F...'s father, and one or two goats for milk, which would do the sick so much good.9

11. I'd like to know whether there's hope you can soon take the sick girl to the Morte. I hope so, don't you? It worries me; being so far away and alone, she can't be properly cared for.10

Goodbye, I'm tired. Yours for ever, affectionate M. R.

1 The account of the debts to be paid has not survived. She hopes

Saint Anne and St Joseph will send the money to pay off those debts, which are fixed in her mind.

2 I was speaking of that one: she had said to hire a daily woman for the washing, because she did not want the postulant who belonged to the Parish Priest to do it;

the Parish Priest's niece, Sr. A. Vincenza writes, without further detail.

3 Anna Carrega. The clothing has been postponed. (Cf. L 209, n. 3). She is to tell Fr Tornatore to write to her.

4 Cf. L 216, n. 6.

5 The Mother does not name the Sister to whom the tasks listed below are to be entrusted. Perhaps she leaves the choice to Sr. A. Vincenza; and from her we know it was Sr. A. Cecilia Tortini.

6 that S.: the Superior Sr. A. Sofia Pasti. She does not seem suited to the task given her.

7 "...to send all the providence (to pay the debts). I'm really waiting for you to come: you'll come with Don Accinelli." Sr. A. Vincenza's absence weighs on her.

8 Considering that the separation weighs even more on Sr. A. Vincenza than on herself, she consoles and encourages her, expressing with affection and faith her special love: my firstborn daughter.

9 the pork. Sr. A. Francesca had given her an exact account of what they had got in hams and salami. The piglets were bought by Sr. A. Francesca's father at Cortemaggiore.

10 that you can take the girl to the House in Via della Morte.

She takes the opportunity of Carlotta's letter, written because she wants a dress; leave it for now, there's time. She awaits news of the solemn inauguration of the Hospital.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I'm taking advantage of Carlotta's wanting to write to you to add a note myself and repeat that you mustn't tire yourself, and should get the nuns of the house to help you so you can have some relief.1

2. I'm afraid my letters are getting lost, for you don't answer one you should have received before the one you mention; for charity's sake tell the postman that if he's not faithful in bringing them to you, you'll give him nothing.2

3. Carlotta is writing to you about the dress, but pay no attention; there's time yet, and meanwhile we go on.3 For charity's sake, if a postulant should turn up, you know, don't you; I'll put no more for fear it gets lost.4

4. I'm waiting to hear that they have solemnly opened the hospital. Give my warm regards to the Mayor and the Secretary, and to the Sisters, and believe me for ever your

Affectionate M. R.

5. And then you'll say I don't write to you; I'm always in credit. Yes, if money comes to you as you say, keep it carefully. Let them attack you. Give my regards to Signora Morando5 and believe me your affectionate M.

1 nuns of the House: of the Sampierdarena Institute. Cf. L 218,1.

2 you won't give him the promised tip.

3 Cf. L 218,5.

4 if a postulant should turn up, keep the money she brings. The reticence is due to fear that letters might be intercepted.

5 Mrs Nina Morando was a friend and benefactress of Mother Rosa and the

FSA Institute.

Her letters bring consolation. Always close, working for Jesus, most faithful Spouse. She is glad she is paying off the debts and suggests various jobs for the house and garden. She does well to keep the postulants in Piacenza; the Mother wants the house full of religious and postulants for the feast of Saint Anne.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I've received your two letters and you can't imagine what consolation they bring me; it's true we are apart, but what do you expect, do you think I'm made of marble and don't feel it? But if we think of doing everything for Jesus, I tell you everything fades away and we find ourselves always united. You say it seemed to you I was close. Yes, my dear, in spirit I'm always with you, and you can live assured that no one but you shares my confidence. Am I alone? no, no — you alone until death! Cheer up, my dear, for the One we serve is a good Father, a most faithful Spouse, incapable of being unfaithful to us; we must not be afraid.1

2. My registered letter may have pained you, seeing what I ordered, but what can we do: God wills it, and so it must be done; let us resign ourselves to his will.2 Tell me, isn't Sr. A. Cherubina at the Morte? she is, isn't she? You answered that person very well; but really! that slip of a girl would only bring us dishonour; you know why.3 Enough; wait for me; for pity's sake have fervent prayers said; I'm trying to obtain a grace, but much prayer is needed.

3. I'm pleased about the Providence; do you know what I do to console myself? Whenever you write that you've paid a bill, I cross it off the list you sent me and at once bless God for it; ah, how often [I say] to my Jesus to send you the money to pay them all! Yes, it will come to you!

4. Everything you've done is very good. Courage! For the stone, you can apply to the Curia, because sending it would cost too much; you can get one for 6 F.4 Next week Sr. A. Michelina and the other will come to Piacenza with the postulant, whom you'll make teacher of the little girls. I'm glad my letter arrived in time to stop that little madcap Sr. A. Geronima going to the S. P. d'Arena house again; she's better off at the Morte; they know her and take her for what she's worth, as the saying goes; whereas that house is known to have enough of them, and besides she's under our eye. I hope she's already at the Morte and won't return to the House.5

5. Poor Countess Caracciolo, she's always our good benefactress.6 It pains me to hear you always write to me after the rosary; I'd like you to go to bed, because then you suffer.7

6. All is going well with Poss; carry on; you did well about the chalice; tell me, did you take the one that was in Ferrara, which will serve for Poss?8

7. Everything you've sent is fine; I'm writing now to Sr. A. Santina to send you the potatoes at once, so she'll do it sooner; she'll send you two sacks; mind you don't hand them all out at once, for you know they must be cut if they're big. For the wire, you could sell all the iron in the cellar and buy wire, or barter it if you think fit; do what you think best; I think the garden will now leave us a surplus, since we'll certainly be taking less.9 You're right, keep the beds; they'll always come in handy.10

8. You tell me Poss doesn't much like those who came from Genoa;11 my dear, you must understand that ours are well brought up and these are rough; once the rust is off, they're just like ours.

9. You do well not to send postulants to Genoa, for I want to fill the house so that by Saint Anne's day there'll be a good number of religious and postulants; with the house well arranged as I told you, it would make a fine showing and Saint Anne would be better honoured.

10. Here it goes on the same way; what madness! Goodbye, I want to post it; now I'll keep a note of those I write to you, and keep those you write to me; yes, I'm (sono) always in credit; today we're even,12 yours for ever, affectionate M. R.

11. I've received these two letters; I'm sorry, you see? meanwhile what does your mother say? Now I'll write a couple of lines of apology, saying I hadn't seen your letter, etc...13

1 Cf. L 220, n. 8.

2 She had told her to stay in Piacenza until Don Accinelli passed through, i.e. the week after Easter. Cf. L 220,8.

3 Sr. A. Cherubina Bartoli. Fr Tornatore had suggested to Sr. A. Vincenza making her Superior of the Mother House, but she had answered that she was too much of a girl; she was 22. Mother Rosa stresses the negative aspects.

4 The altar stone for the altar of the Chapel at the Poss works.

5 Cf. L 216, n. 6; L 220,6.

6 Sr. A. Vincenza, who is having the garden put in order, will ask Countess

Isabella Caracciolo for stakes for the vines.'

7 always after the rosary, which they said in the evening; indeed she generally wrote at 11 p.m. or later.

8 Emilio Poss was pleased with the FSA's work, and Sr. A. Vincenza for her part went on preparing what she could for the chapel.

9 send the potatoes at once for planting in the garden, as they were cheaper in Genoa. For the wire needed to repair the trellises, she advises selling what is in the cellar and bartering it for garden produce, since there is now a surplus, there being fewer Sisters.

10 keep the beds: hold on to them. E. Poss had refused them and preferred to buy camp beds for the girls' dormitories.

11 Poss had described the girls who came from Genoa to work as "lazy, understand nothing, old in years and small in stature".

12 She refers jokingly to the letters she writes and those she receives from Vincenza; today we're even.

13 Sr. A. Vincenza's mother had written; she had kept the letter and told the daughter, but receiving no reply, Signora Rapallino,

worried, had written a second letter. She sends her both. Cf. L

214,11.

She answered Don Accinelli well. The Mother asks prayers for a grace she is awaiting. She is to send Piacenza a quantity of seed potatoes. The Mother wants to know how many Sisters the community now has and whether more are needed.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Today I received your letter. Well done, you answered Don Accinelli well, and it's true: since they are old in vocation, I need them to put in new houses, and the new ones are put in the old houses;1 yes, let us bless God who through St Joseph's intercession sends you so much providence.

2. For charity's sake tell the Sisters to make a novena with communions for me, that God may grant me the [grace] I desire these days. For charity's sake let them pray fervently; commend me to the most fervent.2

3. I'd like you to send about twenty measures of potatoes to Piacenza for planting, as there are none, the few that grew being very poor; I mean you can't find any even to buy; so do me this kindness and send them at once.3

4. How many religious are you? Write and tell me; if you need more I'll send you others; I hear you have postulants at S. P. d'Arena and they'll be clothed, so you'll be able to have them in Genoa. When will you write to me that you're in the big house!4 Goodbye. Give my regards to Alessandro and ask him why he doesn't answer my letters. Warm regards to Don Accinelli; tell him I'll soon send him the paper.5

The Lord bless you with all the others, whom you'll greet for me; your

Affectionate M. R.

1 To Don Accinelli, who objected to three Sisters leaving

Genoa, Sr. A. Santina had replied that the Mother needs old nuns. Yes, adds M. Rosa, Sisters old in vocation are put in new houses, and new Sisters in the old houses.

2 The grace she desires: presumably a successful outcome of the Ricchini case.

3 Cf. L 222, n. 9.

4 In the big house. Cf. L 201, n. 2; 214, n. 12.

5 The original of the permission for the Holy Week services, to have it countersigned by the Archiepiscopal Chancery. (Cf. letter of Accinelli 11.3.1874).

She has seen to the matter he entrusted to her and will send the document as soon as it is ready. The girls will be satisfactorily placed.

A.M.F.

Reverend Parish Priest,

1. A few hours ago I received your esteemed letter together with the certificate, which I sent at once to the Dataria.1 My dear Parish Priest, why didn't you send it to me sooner? You mention the Fr. 10; you should know that this cost more, and as soon as I have the dispensation I'll enclose them in it and send them at once. Believe me, if it had not been for our

Cardinal it would have been much more.2

2. Enough, let's leave it; I hope the girls will be called in the next few days and that Your Reverence will be satisfied with their placement. Please accept the greetings of the Marchioness and of Carlottina and convey them to your excellent wife,4 while I remain

Your Reverence's

Devoted Servant Sr. ANNA ROSA GATTORNO

1 It was evidently a matter of obtaining a dispensation from canonical impediments preventing a couple from celebrating a proper religious marriage.

2 The Institute's Cardinal protector, Luigi Vannicelli, was Pro-Datary, and M.

Rosa had applied to him to obtain the document.

3 D. Bisio, wishing to help the poorer girls of his parish, had secured the Mother's interest. He had written to her on

18.1.1874: "At the end of January I'll send some 20 or 25 girls to Piacenza, most wanting to take the habit, others rescued from bad relatives, others from hunger." The Mother refers here to the young women who will be taken on at the Poss factory.

4 Marchioness Anna Carrega; of Carlotta, who had met him and been his guest; your wife: an obvious error. She certainly meant the Parish Priest's niece, who had gone with him to Piacenza and was a friend of Carlotta's.

As for the two postulants who want to enter, she is to send the details, and the Mother will then reply. She has debts, but the income seems sufficient for a community of only eight Sisters. She asks "special" prayers for a grace.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I've received your letter saying that old woman insists on becoming a nun with the Daughters of Saint Anne, and the younger one too; send me the name and surname, age, dowry and circumstances of both, and then I'll reply accordingly.

2. As for the accounts, listen: you tell me you always have debts; (I) it seems to me that with F. 300 a month you shouldn't run up debts; after all you are so few, 8 religious! For charity's sake, those debts grieve me!1

3. I'm glad of the news of good Cartena;2 blessed be God for it. I'd like the girls, and you too, to say some special prayer for a grace I greatly need.

4. Believe me, there's a mystery about those schoolgirls which the Lord will later reveal.3 My health isn't very good; I can barely stand; your affectionate M. R. Greet all the Sisters for me; (whom) God bless them all.

1 with F. 300 a month: Countess Maria Anna Trotti's subsidy.

2 It is not clear who she is.

3 A mystery. The Countess had issued various prohibitions: the girls were not to go on the grand staircase, in the entrance hall, etc. The reason had to be discovered, and who was advising her.

She asks her to buy and send the things she lists and to give everything to Don Accinelli, who will pass through Piacenza. As for letters, she cannot say Vincenza is in credit. She is to be careful to pay the quarterly taxes.

A.M.F.

My daughter for ever,

1. I hope you've received my registered letter and another one also addressed to you.1 Now I come begging for a little chocolate, because here it's far too dear; a shopping basket, one of the cheap ones, you know, the kind Sr. A. Nazzarena always buys; some fine cotton to make socks, not too tightly twisted, otherwise they end up stiff(?); half a dozen, you know, for Anna; 6 will be enough.2

2. The potatoes will reach you soon; make sure the beans are the kind that don't climb, you know, the dwarf ones that stay low and give a lot.3

3. When Accinelli passes through4 you can give him a little salami, not much, because they eat it up here; one or two at most. You can put all the things you send me in Father Agostino's suitcase, for he wants it; put in a few handkerchiefs with a border, one for Carlotta — I know she wants them; she'll treasure them and won't say.

4. Then you'll say I'm not in credit; well, now I'm keeping count: I wrote to you on Sunday and today, and you've written to me only on Sunday. It's true I received two; enough, I'm saying it in fun.5

5. Please keep an eye on the taxes payable every three months; if by mischance they've fallen due, you see, there's a fine; for charity's sake watch out.

6. I hope you've written to Don Accinelli to bring you the house papers; for charity's sake write it tactfully and make him understand you need them, so he isn't offended, for he has already taken very badly what you wrote him about the religious;6 you know well. I'll say no more, for I know this is enough for you.

7. That Person receives 4 of my letters, answers (one) half of one, and that's all.7 Bravo! I'll do the same. Goodbye, my dear; I'm finishing because Carlotta is waiting to go out.

Your affectionate M. R.

1 These are: L 220; 222.

2 a shopping basket; if they end up sticche: perhaps too stiff; for

Anna Carrega.

3 The potatoes will be sent from Genoa (cf. L 223,3). The beans to be planted in the garden should be non-climbing.

4 He was to go to Rome for Anna Carrega's clothing (cf. L 209,5).

Carlotta... won't say we neglect her.

5 Cf. L 222, n. 12.

6 you wrote him: she had told him on the Mother's behalf that some Sisters were to be moved from Genoa.

7 Fr Tornatore.

She has received news of the hospital's opening and thanks God, sole author of all good. She wants her always to keep Sr. A. Angiola in her community and to send her the money through Alessandro. She has had heavy expenses and wants to leave something for communities with no resources. She is to have the Archbishop invited to bless the Chapel.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Yesterday I received your letter telling me at last that the opening of the hospital went well.1 Thanks be to God for it, the author and maker of all good. My dear, God give you strength to do everything well for him alone; we want no other, do we? Now let's talk about the Sisters: you tell me you have Sr. A. Angiola with you; it would be good if you kept her always, so that with you there'd be fewer C...2

2. Something else I'd like you to do: I hear some postulants came with money; you'd need to tell the Superior to hand it over to you (te), because you would get it to me.3 Understood? If this happened before Alessandro came to Rome, you could give it to him well wrapped and tell him to say nothing (che) and bring it to me; understood?

3. My dear Francesca, you surely can't believe what this poor mother of yours is going through, and far away from you two, the only ones (of) to whom I can say a word; alas, I must always be like a thief, careful over my smallest words! Sickness, deaths, accounts — an abyss of expenses, and now the V...of A... For charity's sake try to do as I say above.4

4. I'm writing to Alessandro now and telling him to do it properly and let no one notice. Imagine, you see, I've been here three months; the bills I've paid were no small matter, and I still have one with Fr Agostino; I've given him most of it. Enough; I hope St Joseph will send it to me to leave to these houses, which have, my dear, no resources at all.5

5. I hope you'll now see about having the Archbishop come; tell the Mayor that one is obliged to inform him every time a Chapel is opened, and then go and invite him, asking him to come and bless the hospital and the little Chapel; tell Don Accinelli to let him know too.6 I hope all will go well. Goodbye.

6. As for the two houses having lent you things for the Chapel, I'm surprised, since everything belongs to Saint Anne. It's needed!7 Enough, you'll soon have everything; I have a fine pyx, a fine chalice and [a] fine chasuble that serves for all colours.

Your affectionate M. for ever M. R.

1 The letter is of 17 March. The solemn opening, attended by the highest authorities and many people, had taken place on 15 March.

2 you have Sr. A. Angiola Degrossi with you, of the Sampierdarena community; if you kept her always she'd be with you, apart from Sr. A. Cecilia Tortini.

not a little in teaching the girls, because of the deafness that had struck her some time before.

3 to the Superior Augusta Biagini.

4 you are the only ones: the closest collaborators, the most responsibly committed and trusted. She must constantly watch her words to avoid misunderstandings and gossip; she cannot allow herself to unburden herself, though weighed down by so many troubles: sick

Sisters, deaths, debts. And now the V... of A.: Anna Carrega's clothing involved expense and work. Cf. L 228,3. Try to do as she said above,

in paragraph 2.

5 Money was needed for the Rome houses, which had very meagre income.

She had borrowed from Fr Agostino and repaid him. She hopes in providence to be able to leave a little help for communities without resources.

6 Cf. L. 207, n. 4.

7 There had been complaints from the Sisters of the Sampierdarena and Genoa houses. She is surprised but concludes simply with two words, it's needed! and enough. She would send her all she had.

She begs her never to speak of the Rules to anyone. She asks her to send the cloth needed for Anna Carrega's clothing. She is glad to hear she has almost no debts left; she awaits the moment she is entirely free of them to sing the Te Deum; then she can send her some money.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I hope you're back, so I'm writing to you at Piacenza. For charity's sake, my dear Vincenza, don't talk about the Rules to anyone at all; what you write that that person told you to do about it alarmed me — my God! Do nothing, think nothing; whoever is in a calm harbour certainly can't understand what happens to someone in the middle of a stormy sea. Calm your ideas and remember that the good God is doing what pleases him.1

2. Quick, get on with the tasks I wrote to you about; I'd like them done promptly; for now think of nothing else.2

3. Listen, I need you to send me everything needed for Anna's Clothing, as things are very dear in this city, and there's the burden of so many expenses you know of, the bills I had to pay and the huge expenses I have now. In Trastevere there are two sick Sisters, Sr. A. Benvenuta and Sr. A. Michelina; what expense! The illness, God alone knows.3 So send me enough serge for two habits, cotton for two underskirts, a little tibet to make 2 scapulars for her, and cotton for an apron, two large veils, two small ones, two aprons. You've understood, haven't you?

4. My dear, how many troubles weigh on me, and alone, without even you to say a word to; I must hide everything and let no one notice; the worst is that I'm surrounded; you understand me, enough. May God assist us; we shall go on living until the day of our blessed death.4

5. If you knew how glad I am to read that soon there won't be a cent of debt! I keep crossing off and can really see we're near the end; ah, good God, how you console me on this side!5 I'd like St Joseph to send you enough to buy the things I've written about without running into debt; I'd truly appreciate it. I can't wait to come back; as soon as Anna is clothed I'll come;6 I await your letters and am your

affectionate M. ROSA

Acknowledge all the letters you've received, to see whether [any] has been lost.

6. I've just received your letter telling me so many good things about the new house; blessed be God who deigned to turn his gaze upon us; in all you have done I have always been with you.7

7. Tell me, what does the Chemist's bill for the two years come [to]? You know nearly half is taken off; write and tell me. Oh, blessed day when you tell me: "Mother, they're all settled!" I assure you I'll run to the feet of Jesus to say the Te Deum; then you can send me something, as I have to send 4 people down: one lay person, a very good postulant, and the others religious — the two sick Sisters and Sr. A. Crocifissa; put these three at the Morte; let that one be well watched there... enough.8

8. How dreadful, all the money Sr. Tommasina spends! what, she has nothing, with only a handful of them? well done!9

9. See whether Count Scotti,10 who had promised to supply the medicines for our girls free... If he has forgotten, ask him to grant them. It would be a great help.

Goodbye, your affectionate MOTHER on earth and in Heaven, yours.

Tell that person that now...11

1 You'll be back. She had gone to Cortemaggiore to conclude the contract for the hospital. Don't speak of the Rules... storm. Sr. A. Vincenza reassures her on

21 March: "Rest quite easy... that person (Fr Tornatore) did want me to take them (the Rules) to the Bishop; I said no, and that he too should take care not to speak of them to anyone."

2 Cf. L 220; 222; 226.

3 Sr. A. Benvenuta Grino and Sr. A. Michelina Morelli: she had decided to send them to Piacenza to be better cared for in the infirmary.

4 She also revealed her state of mind to Sr. A. Francesca, cf. L 227,3.

5 Cf. L 220,1.

6 As soon as Anna Carrega is clothed. The clothing had been set for 25

March; it was later postponed to 19 April. Cf. L 231,7.

7 Cf. letter of Sr. A. Vincenza to M. Rosa of 17 March 1874.

8 Sr. A. Crocifissa Fiocchi. Put them: send them to the infirmary in Via della Morte.

9 Sr. A. Tommasina Viterbo was spending too much for few people.

10 Among the members of the noble Piacenza family this is certainly Guglielmo

Scotti Douglas, a Piacenza town councillor for many years and for 14 years

President of the Congregation of Charity. Cf. L 5.

11 She does not finish the message for Fr Tornatore.

She is greatly consoled to hear how the heavenly Father shows his goodness and mercy. They must respond by keeping the Rules.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Your letters are the greatest consolation to me:1 how good God is! how indebted we are, my (my) [dear], to this most merciful Father!

2. Let us try to satisfy and respond to such goodness by keeping our holy Rules; the good God wants nothing else, for if we do this we shall give him great pleasure.

3. So everything depends on you; courage, then. Write and tell me how many you are now; I'd like to know.

Goodbye. Greet everyone for me, and may the Lord bless you; and you in particular believe me your affectionate M. R.

1 the greatest consolation. St Joseph keeps sending providence; the Sisters are good and observant and are making a name as fine nurses in caring for the sick. Cf. letters of Solenghi to M. Rosa: 8.3.74 and 13.3.74.

She has written to Don Accinelli, sending him the uncle's letter. She has had a letter from the Father and wants to know whether he received a letter enclosed in a registered one she sent. She urges her to have the work on the house done and to send the things requested earlier.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I've just finished reading yours, with your uncle's enclosed; I had written to Don Accinelli to appeal and I hope he has done so; now I've written to him and sent him your letter, or rather your uncle's.1

2. I hope you're back in Piacenza, for I'm very anxious.2 Listen, that person has just written to me; I'd like to know whether he received the letter that was in your registered one; I'm worried; you acknowledged it but he didn't; what a torment, my dear! For charity's sake acknowledge my letters; I keep a record.3

3. You've done everything well about the money and the provisions, and the rest. Now set to work at once on what I told you in the registered letter; it's all work that can be done in a month.4

4. I hope you've received the others, including the one asking you to send me the things for Anna, as soon as you can, because it takes time before everything is done. Don't forget to include two dozen manuals of Saint Anne.5

5. The storms are growing, my dear; I'm right in the midst of thorns; enough! I'm still standing.6 Goodbye, my dear; what a sacrifice it is for me to be far from you! Patience! Goodbye, your affectionate M. R.

1 Cf. L 216,4.

2 Sr. A. Vincenza had spent some days at Cortemaggiore for the hospital contract.

3 She is anxious, fearing that her letters to Fr Tornatore and the

Sisters may fall into other hands.

4 Work in the garden and reorganization of the house.

5 to send me the things: L 228,3. The Manuals, cf. L 192, n. 6.

6 Problems of every kind, cf. 228,4, and especially over the Rules.

She replies at once. Francesca is to have the doctor examine the two girls and take the appropriate decisions. The Mother has had a letter from the Mayor; Francesca is to insist on the contract being drawn up. She may decide about accepting the postulant, but is not to accept girls who have been in service. Right after Anna Carrega's clothing on 19 April the Mother hopes to leave Rome.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I hope you've now received my letter; I was slow to write because I was waiting for letters from you; I'd had none for 8 days; as soon as I got one I answered at once, as I'm doing now, replying to yours received this morning, though I'm extremely busy.

2. First let me tell you about the girl with that nasty illness. Listen: get a doctor's certificate for her, because she's from Sestri and is going to the Genoa hospital; at once, without losing time; as for the other, if it's nothing much, let them keep her; if not, out, without human respect, since this girl came with such an illness; you answered the Rev. Parish Priest excellently.1

3. I hope Defilippi will come, and then, after the retreat, another will be appointed, for I don't like this one.2

4. Bravo, Mayor! he wrote that the altar has been quite finished for more than 20 days. See about making the contract; tell him I wrote to you about it; I've written to him too, but it's all yes and then nothing gets done. Listen, I'd like them to make it for at least five years; I'll write to him tomorrow.3

5. As for the postulant, I leave you free to do as you think best; if you see she can be useful, accept her; first have your doctor examine her, for I wouldn't want her missing teeth to be due to scurvy; if she's healthy you can accept her. Servants, no, for charity's sake.4

6. If it could be arranged for the two vipers to go to Genoa when the bigger house opens, they could go then. What a consolation and stroke of luck for that house!5

7. My dear daughter, I can't bear being in Rome any longer; on 19 April Anna is clothed, and then I leave at once. I long to see you, but there's still a month before I leave.6 Please don't tire yourself. Goodbye, your affectionate

M. R.

1 that nasty illness: scabies; the other girl is to be treated at home. "The Parish

Priest of Promontorio (?), egged on by the two vipers" (the Vernengos), had proposed moving the Superior Augusta as too young. Sr. A. Francesca had replied that there was no need to change her: "I know the Superior and she is not as they make her out". (Cf. letter of F. Camisa 19.3.74).

2 Cf. L 206, n. 9.

3 The Mayor does not keep his word either about the chapel or the contract.

4 The Rules forbade accepting girls who had been in service.

5 the two vipers, as Sr. A. Francesca wrote. It would be good (what a consolation!) for the Sampierdarena community to move them to the Genoa community once it has the bigger house. Cf. L 201, n. 2; 214, n. 12; 223, n. 4.

6 Anna Carrega. Cf. L 228, n. 6.

She sends two letters to be delivered. She explains how to rearrange three rooms and put others in order. She announces the arrival of two postulants from Ferrara. She urges the Sister cook to take care in preparing the Sisters' food.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I'm answering yours at once and enclosing one for Poss and another for the archpriest of Cortemaggiore, whose address I don't have; look at it, address it and post it, and take the one for Poss to him; read that one first too and then take it to him; understand?

2. Listen, the papers you mention in yours are fine; but I meant the taxes that fall due (of) every two or three months, which incur a fine if not paid.1

3. Now the infirmary: for charity's sake leave it as it is; why do you want to make it a dormitory? I think that for the girls there are it must be enough; I hope you have only a few (che), three or four; so leave it as it is and put them there provisionally. Later I'll tell you what to do.2

4. Try to get everything done quickly and keep in front of you the paper I sent, where it's all described in detail how you are to arrange the three upstairs rooms; once these are done, the builders can use the kitchen stairs to raise those two.3

5. Let our room be ready, and yours and Carlotta's. By ours I mean the Superior's, for I can already see I'm so crippled that I shan't always be able to stay on my feet and go to my beloved little room.4 Patience! Ah, if only I could at least die there!

6. From Ferrara you'll receive an elderly qualified teacher who will serve as novice mistress this year, and another who is young; you'll see her. For now put them in those upstairs rooms near the privy.

7. Make sure at Poss that the girls are well supervised, and put more nuns there;5 I didn't quite understand what you say about writing to Mancini.6

8. Listen: servants, no, absolutely not! I don't want them, because God wills it so. The one I'm sending you from here is from a very good family, a dear person; you'll see her.

9. Tell Sr. A. Nazzarena not to feed us badly, for everyone in general complains about the cooking in Piacenza; let her know she is cooking for the servants of the Lord, not for pigs.

10. You're right that I have many consolations; what can I say, I realize it's my bad character.7 As for the Rules, being here is one thing, being far away another, where one judges without seeing.

Your affectionate M.

1 In her letter of 21 March Sr. A. Vincenza had written that she had asked Don

Accinelli for "the papers she needed for the Cortemaggiore contract". The Mother had urged her to watch for tax payment notices:

cf. L 226,5.

2 I think that for the present number of girls it must be enough;

I hope you have few, three or four.

3 keep in front of you the paper for restructuring the rooms. She had made her a sketch (the paper), without which it is impossible to follow her suggestions about the work.

4 My beloved little room: the small room still kept intact as in her day.

5 put more nuns there: add other Sisters for the smooth running.

6 Sr. A. Vincenza had asked her: "Should I write to Don Alessandro Mancini about those young women he wrote he has, who want to become Daughters of Saint Anne but have been in service for a while?" The Mother's answer is negative. Cf. L 231,5 and the relevant note.

7 To console her she wrote (on 21.3.74): "Mother has enormous sorrows but also consolations. I hear the praise given to the Sampierdarena hospital... and to Cortemaggiore, and isn't that a consolation to you? The sick say they are in paradise when they are in hospital."

She explains how to arrange certain rooms for the community, postulants and novices, and the improvements to be made to some rooms. She announces the arrival of two Sisters and a postulant from Rome.

A.M.F.

My Vincenza,

1. Pay attention to what (ti) I'm about to tell you. The ground-floor room where the lamps were, the big one — I mean the empty one between the two rooms with the looms — empty it, then call the whitewasher and have it well whitewashed; when it's dry, move the girls' school there, all the benches, the papers, everything in short; arrange them as best you can, and I want it nicely set out; for now, the handful of girls there are2 can be kept in the room where they wash in the morning; understood?

2. Now the school, which will be empty: put there the three beds in the big room that have curtains round them, and the other two in the Superior's room, making 5; one without a curtain, which must be [in the] infirmary, put in the end room, where it will stand alone without curtains; that is, three in the first room and two in the second.

3. First have them well whitewashed, the stove properly repaired and the windows made to shut tight; in the big room put an iron bed for yourself, freshly painted, and likewise for the Superior — let the bed be freshly painted — and have it placed in the middle of the room where the chest of drawers is, putting the chest to one side,

so I want the big room nicely arranged with its bed in the middle and the two chests of drawers — in short, well ordered.

4. For the moment don't (ce le) let the girls go into the school. Call the builder and have him put the big room where the girls now sleep in good repair, opening another window where the mark is, and set it in order with chairs round the walls, a small table, a well-made wooden bed and a chest of drawers; (and this) and once whitewashed this is to serve as the nurses' school.

5. The next room will be for the novices; have it properly repaired and whitewashed, enlarging the small high window under the roof. The novices will work there; put (le) a new table in the middle and a small one for the mistress; in that sort of niche make (le) a pretty little altar and put Saint Anne there — I'll send you the statue, you know, the one they dressed for me.3

6. In the first room off the big room have the window lowered and the builder fit an iron balcony to give more light, and make a white curtain for it from the underskirts there; there too put tables round the walls, with a table for the postulants; buy chairs like the white ones we have in our workroom.

7. The two sloping rooms — you know, where the potatoes were — well, when the builder has finished what (che) I've told you above, have them raised and made straight, with an extra window where the wall is raised, and these two will serve for our recreation; furnish them well with chairs and a table in the middle of each.

8. Now let's see where you're to put those two little girls with the teacher: in the infirmary, and in the two rooms next to the privy, you know, don't you? But I hope they'll all be in the infirmary, and you can keep these two rooms for some rather more ladylike postulant, such as the one I'll send you soon,

whom you can make teacher of the little girls, and also to sleep there; and make Sr. A. Giovanna mistress of the postulants who sleep by the privy, in that long dormitory where the girls used to be, next to the washroom; I think

I've explained myself well enough.

9. Where you don't understand, write and tell me; and keep this letter of mine in front of you and do what it says. I hope you'll have all these things done promptly, so that when I come I can set up the noviciate and postulancy.

10. If the cost isn't too great, it would be good to lower the three windows of the nurses' schoolroom and fit iron balconies to these too, for more light; what do you think? You'll see; if it's too expensive, leave them for now and have the other one opened, beside the closed conical one; what do you think of my plan? I intend to leave Rome soon, as soon as Anna is clothed.4

11. I hope you'll get this before leaving for Cortemaggiore. Listen: with the postulant the two nurses will also come, Sr. A. Benvenuta and Sr. A. Michelina; send these two to the Morte.5

12. I haven't had a letter from you for two days. For charity's sake write and tell me how you are, for I'm always worried about your cough, knowing you don't look after yourself. Goodbye, your affectionate M. R.

1 The date is inferred from the context.

2 that handful of girls: three or four, cf. L 232,3.

3 niche: a recess in the wall; put the statue of Saint Anne there.

4 As soon as Anna Carrega is clothed, i.e. after 19 April. Cf. L 231,7.

5 Cf. L 222,4; L 228, n. 3.

As soon as she received the money order she ran to the Chapel to thank the Lord. She answers some questions and gives instructions for work in the house. Appealing to the example of Jesus, she extols his charity, which inspires her in full trust in providence. She attended the ceremony erecting the Congregation of the Children of Mary at the Fornaci.

A.M.F.

My dear daughter,

1. I've just received yours with the money order for F. 300 and went at once to prostrate myself at the feet of my God to thank him; may he ever be blessed for it! Yesterday I didn't write because I was very breathless; today it's better; you can't imagine what consolation your letter brought me.

2. I'll answer everything. Listen: for now I'd leave the stove, but if you see it's no good, take it out and have it put where you think best. As for the altar, have it pulled down; meanwhile the [...] will serve you.1

3. For the work on the two rooms, before starting, get an estimate from the builder, see what he says and write to me. As for the balconies, yes, yes, let him make them.

4. You say raising the rooms will take two months; very well, as long as it's finished before Saint Anne's. We should see whether the postulants' refectory could be enlarged by knocking down the wall into the room where they make the salami. Ask the builder; that way it would be just right; what do you think? Otherwise you did well.

5. Tell that person that Poss cannot deceive us, because we're covered, and that these wicked tongues are counting on the bones of charity, because now it's dead, especially among religious; they trample this most excellent and precious jewel underfoot and can do nothing but reckon up good eating. Ah, if only I could once see them all stuffed with this eating up to their eyes!2

6. My dear daughter, forgive me this outburst, but when I hear religious talk of this repulsive eating, my nerves catch fire and I can't contain myself; it really harms my health. Ah, Jesus, who went into the desert drawing the crowds after him, never thought that there was nothing to eat there, but thought rather of feeding their souls. And what did he have? what did they give him? Why didn't he think of his apostles, who were poor? What was their future? The Providence of God!

7. "Ah, dear Good, I have given food, I have spread your word — everything on the wings of Providence!"3

8. Surely that person didn't write this note; if he did, he was forced to, for his principles are different.4

9. Whatever Mr Poss does will be as it will be; meanwhile we feed them, rescue them from sin, teach them [to] love God! The Eternal Father will see to the rest. What do we have here, my dear? Who gave us the income to provide soup for these hungry girls? God!5

10. I hope you've received my letter with the two lines for Poss; yes, my dear, prudence yes, but not the sort of prudence of today, where to do a little charity we religious must be paid up front. How dreadful, what a wrong spirit! Our saint, who [is] full of charity, dislikes it — she abhors it.6

11. Courage, forward; here I'm accepting postulants as fast as I can. You ask about the clothings; do as you like; I approve whatever you do. Listen, my dear Vincenza: you've sent me F. 300; I'd written to Alessandro that when he came to Piacenza he would collect them and bring them to me. If I go to the Loreto house I'll call you; I'd like you first to do what I wrote to you, then you'll come to fetch me, and meanwhile bring me some religious. I really hope to send them to you by Saturday.7

12. Listen, send me some tickets for the southern line. It costs much less; meanwhile tell me exactly what you spent from Rome to Piacenza; write to me at once; I'm waiting for the things, for time is short.8

13. Listen, you who saw with me the marble basin with taps at the nuns', I'd like you to have one put between the two windows, you know, in the lamp room, with its sink underneath and a pipe leading out into the garden; have I explained? See what it costs.9

14. Now think of laying in some provisions: coal, flour, maize and whatever else is needed.

15. Rest assured you won't lack postulants; in a few days two will come from Ferrara. In Trastevere they want to know when you paid for the coal.10 If you remember, write and tell me; if not, don't worry; it's always the same house. God grant it goes well. The soups here are going marvellously; see what providence!

16. Yesterday I attended a magnificent ceremony at the Fornaci, though I could hardly stand; they erected the congregation of the Children of Mary; Mgr Negrotto conferred the medals; procession; they were all dressed in white; sermon; soon they'll set it up at the Parrocchietta too.11 Goodbye, my dear Vincenza. When Carlotta saw the money order she jumped for joy, because now I'll buy her everything she wrote to you about. She's beside herself with delight. Goodbye again; I hope you'll come and join me.

Your affectionate M. ROSA

1 she does not finish the thought.

2 Tell Fr Tornatore that Poss cannot deceive us... It was rumoured in

Piacenza that Poss wanted to exploit the situation by paying little. Mother Rosa goes beyond human calculation, guided by charity and the Gospel; she looks to the one model: Christ.

3 Jesus by his life clearly shows her the criteria to follow.

4 Surely Fr Tornatore, moved by principles of charity, cannot have written this note. (The note in question has not survived).

5 Mr Poss has a mentality of interest and profit; but our aim is to help and benefit these girls in body and soul, trusting in the Eternal Father.

6 my letter with the two lines for Poss: L 232. She concludes her remarks on the motives inspiring the FSA's charitable action: prudence yes, but generous openness of heart. Saint Anne, full of charity, abhors the human self-interest that seeks payment up front.

7 I'd like you to: she should do what was written, accompanying to the infirmary in Via della Morte the two Sisters the Mother will send as soon as possible. Cf. L 233,11.

8 some reduced-fare tickets for the southern railways. Sr. A. Vincenza writes her the cost of the Rome–Florence tickets, without reduction, and Florence–

Piacenza with the reduction.

9 She has found out the cost of the marble basin seen at the nuns of Tor de' Specchi: 75 francs. And she comments: "Just what was needed for washing! So much for poor Daughters of Saint Anne — we're getting rich, without a cent. What a laugh!

I'm almost broke, unless Saint Anne sends me some." (Letter of 23.3.74 to M. Rosa).

10 She had not paid for the coal.

11 The Mother cared greatly about erecting the Congregation of the Children of Mary for the Christian formation of girls.

She reassures her, urging her not to worry if she cannot send money and to lead the community as she feels inspired. She asks her to take charge of how the other community is run, helping and advising the Superior.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I'm answering your two letters, which I received together this morning; you say I tell you nothing about the postulant; read carefully: see what I told you to do — whatever you think best; I repeat it.1

2. Don't worry too much about sending me money; if it comes to you, send it; if not, God will send it to me from elsewhere.

3. I note what you say about Augusta, but for now I really don't wish to, for my own good reasons.2 As for the man, do as you think best; indeed it's my wish that you act as you feel inspired, for I like you to act [responsibly].3 I'd only point out that it would be good for you to go to the Archbishop too.4 Keep Sr. A. Apollonia as rested as possible; for charity's sake don't let her go out, and spare her the night duty if you can.

4. You tell me you've sent me lots of things, but I can't send for them because I have no receipt.5 For now keep an eye on that house yourself and tell the Superior to do what you teach her and do nothing without first consulting you. Nothing more for now, because I want to (le) post it; your

Affectionate M. R.

1 Your two letters: both of 25 March. About the postulant,

she had answered clearly: cf. 231,5.

2 I note what you say about Augusta: this Superior behaves "really like a girl"... Don Accinelli is utterly fed up with Sr. A. Augusta.

But the Mother thinks it best not to intervene for now, especially as Sr.

A. Francesca is advising and helping her. See below, par. 4.

3 As for the man: a male nurse from the Cortemaggiore hospital recommended by the doctor for her to take on. The Mother reminds her of her responsibility, since the Mayor has "left her the choice of nurses".

4 It would be good for you to go in person. Sr. A. Francesca wanted to send the hospital chaplain to invite him. (Cf. L 207,5; 227,5).

5 She had sent her "mint water, pasta, chocolate".

She sends Easter greetings and thanks her for the good she does to her Daughters in Ferrara. Her reward is already assured in heaven at a hundred per cent.

A.M.F.

My most beloved Sister,

1. I hope you received mine dated the 16th of this month.2 Before wishing you a happy Easter, I want to thank you for what you do for your daughters in Ferrara; I too share great consolation in seeing them so loved and helped by you; your wage is secured in the Bank of Paradise; one day up there you'll find a return of a hundred per cent.3

2. Yes, you are God's favourite; oh, how many there are who like you could buy themselves a palace in Paradise and so pass from one to the other! Instead they let all their wealth run riot in the soil here below, like the spring flower that dies when summer comes; so they too, at the end of their life, fall to the earth and all is over; and most dreadful of all, on the painful journey they will make they will find only reproaches, and their own goods will be their accusers.

3. You, my dear — what a lot is yours! The Daughters of Saint Anne will come to meet you with their holy Mother Saint Anne, and thus escorted by the little girls bearing the emblem of charity they will lead you before God's throne to receive the reward of your sufferings and of the charity you have practised so long. May God let you taste his resurrection, which I wish you with all affection, while I remain for life your

Unworthy Servant and Sister Sr. ANNA ROSA GATTORNO

1 The addressee is missing, but from the content, the epistolary style and manner of address it is clearly Countess Trotti.

2 The letter mentioned is missing.

3 Easter fell on 5 April. Your daughters: the Sisters of the Ferrara community. With fine psychological insight she calls them hers, as if to remind her of the commitment she had made to help the community financially.

Countess Maria Anna Trotti.

Yes, the washbasins must be marble. She has done everything well. The Mother has neglected writing because she has been ill. She asks her to tell the Father she has received all his letters and that Princess Colonna has died.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I'm answering your last letter, received on Thursday the 2nd.1 You ask whether the washbasins must all be marble: yes, all of them, and everything in marble.

2. You did well about Maddalena; I approve everything;2 leave Sr. A. Giovanna sleeping in her little room, and Colomba where you've put her, and the vice-superior too.3

3. I'm pleased with how you've arranged things. If they don't dissuade her, a fine postulant will come on the 2nd, and she'll make an excellent Superior there: a great lady of most noble manners, very well educated.4

4. My dear Vincenza, these days I've really longed for you; the breathlessness came on and I'm still not over it; I had to apply two blisters; the fluid they released, and still release, is a fountain, but the pain has eased [a] little, and the breathlessness too. If you see Albertazzi, ask what he says about this fluid; it weakens me terribly.5 Then what I have to suffer from the...6 Enough, I'll write nothing; only that I'd like you near me, because

I really don't know how I am.

5. I hope you've received my registered letter. It's

5 days since I last had a letter from you. Tell that person that I've received all his, and I hope mine have reached him; I'm not writing to him any more because I feel ill. Tell him Princess Colonna has died intestate and without even being able to receive the Sacraments; that's what comes of waiting on his inspirations, wanting it just like the M.sa A.7 Goodbye, I am your affectionate M. Rosa

1 Sr. A. Vincenza's letter is of 29 March.

2 About Maddalena: Mrs Parmigiani, who had placed her house in

Cortemaggiore at the disposal of the Daughters of Saint Anne so they could nurse the sick at home. Cf. App. IV. Cortemaggiore.

3 Sr. A. Giovanna Bixio, Sr. A. Colomba Chianale, the vice-superior Sr. A.

Carmelita Romainone.

4 on the 2nd of this month, meaning: on 2 May a fine postulant will come, Maria

Fantini, a widow born in 1830. She entered the Institute on 3 May 1874. Cf. Reg. Post.,

n. 240.

5 Sante Albertazzi, the community doctor.

6 suffer from the... She leaves the sentence unfinished. Perhaps she means: the Sisters.

7 Tell Fr Tornatore... I'm not writing to him. He, with his inspirations... Probably Fr Tornatore had hoped Princess Colonna would leave something in her will to the Daughters of Saint Anne, as he hopes from Marchioness Fanny

Anguissola Visconti.

She is not to go to Albaro to the Lady she had mentioned. She thanks the Sisters and asks them to pray for a grace.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Just a line to tell you that neither you nor the others are to go any more to that lady at Albaro; I meant to write to you earlier to warn you not to go, but what can I say, I haven't had a moment; enough, it's done now; don't go again, understood?1 Thank the dear religious for me and tell them to pray for something, the reason for which the Superior will tell you later.2

Goodbye. Greet everyone and Don Accinelli for me, and believe me

your affectionate M. R.

2. I hope Don Accinelli has received a letter of mine.

Get rid of your temptation that you'll be sent away. What nonsense; you mustn't think of it.3

1 Sr. A. Santina replies on 8.4 that she will be obeyed. "As soon as Don

Accinelli comes she'll tell him." Cf. L 239,1.

2 The Superior: Sr. A. Francesca Camisa.

3 A real temptation. There was no reason to think so.

4 to... that lady, as Sr. A. Santina writes, is a certain Prato Longo, gravely ill and often visited by the Archbishop. That is why the Mother advises the Sisters to go to her early in the morning.

She is to give Alessandro a bottle of the decoction. The Mother is glad to hear they will soon be in the new house. Recommendations for the Sisters.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Today I received your letter, as I hope you've received mine; I'm answering to tell you not to go to the Durazzo lady.1 Listen, give Alessandro a bottle of the decoction to put in his suitcase; otherwise send me nothing else, for there's everything here.2

2. I'm very glad to hear you'll soon be in the new house.3 God bless his work. Goodbye, my dear; greet everyone for me, God bless you, and believe me your affectionate M. R.

3. For charity's sake don't let the religious fail to go to... that

Lady4 whom you say the Archbishop visits; let them go early in the morning, for charity's sake, so there's no cause for complaint.

Goodbye, yours.

Warm regards to Don Accinelli.

1 This is the lady she wrote about in L 238,1.

2 Alessandro was to go to Rome (cf. L 209,5). She needs only the decoction prepared by Signora Maddalena Bacigalupo. Sr. A. Santina replies (on 11

April) that the lady is preparing not one but four bottles.

3 I'm very glad. The Sisters now number fifteen and Don Accinelli has managed to find a roomier house. "This evening," writes Santina, "they're giving him the key of the House, so on Monday (13 April) he'll send the builders in" to whitewash it.

So the problem is solved. Cf. L 231, n. 5.

4 to... that Lady: as Sr. A. Santina writes, a certain Prato Longo, seriously ill and often visited by the Archbishop. This is why the Mother urges the Sisters to go to her early in the morning.

She urges her to send off the two postulants at once and to press those who are studying to obtain their diploma.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I was slow to answer your letter asking about the young postulant; well, do as you write: let them pay this money in the instalments you indicate, and let them leave at once, for I don't want them staying in that house.1

2. For charity's sake let the two who are to take the diploma study, for I'm counting on it, and I hope the teacher will get them ready to pass, for the elementary one doesn't take much. Have prayers said, for I'm unwell2 your affectionate M. R.

1 Besides the "old" postulant, a young one had come forward (cf. L 225,1). Her parents would send the money for expenses in instalments: L. 100 in June, September and December.

2 The two student Sisters: Sr. A. Irene Carmeli and Sr. A. Beatrice Merici. (Cf. letter of Bucciotti to M. Rosa 11.4.74).

She suggests where to place certain pieces of furniture and gives her view on some questions about the work to be done. She wants news of the Father and to know whether Vincenza has been to the Vicar to have the letter about him written. Anna wants the stockings.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Today I received yours acknowledging my unstamped letter, in which you go to such pains to convince me of what I was already more than convinced of, and there was no need even to tell that person, since you put a wrapper on it and that was that. Can you still doubt and think I might suppose you could ever betray me? Naughty girl!1

2. Listen, now to the work. You ask about having it painted and say the whole corridor will cost F. 50; well, it's better to spend it; it's necessary, so it must be done; God will see to it; have it painted.

3. So listen: the wardrobes in the corridor — you know, the three black ones — I'd like you to remove them, because they look bad in corridors; put one, the one half full of cloth and half of Carlotta's dresses, in your room; the other two downstairs, one in the room where we work, where the big chest of drawers is, and the other big one where the blankets go in the lamp room, where you're having the marble basin put; and the sofa there, out with it too, put it downstairs in the parlour; in short, the main corridor as far as St Francis must be empty. Those two gilt ones,2 leave them where they are, for they look well.

4. I've written yes to painting the door. If you see that the tracetta curtains3 are needed, have them made. I'd like the builders to finish the upstairs rooms quickly; the kitchen whitewash can wait; we'll have it done when things are further on.

5. I'd like you to try to keep few girls and send them all to Poss, so that there are as few as possible in the house.

6. You don't mention that person any more, and from the way you write I think you've had a row, haven't you? What happened? write and tell me. I hope you've received mine telling you to go to the Vicar and ask him to tell the Bishop too, provided he writes it well and not like last year's; you can tell that person so.4

7. I've arranged the opening of another house in Perugia, and we'll go there when I come down. I'm held captive here and don't know what to do. One fine day I'll just leave everything and come away. I'm tired.

8. Listen, about Signora Iussi's girl,5 note that she has sent me F. 100 once and for all and wants her to go into the factory; this for your guidance. I'd like all the good ones to go there; I'm waiting for the letter to see whether I get anywhere, and then I'll come away.6

9. I'm much better; but I always keep a blister open and find it does me good; when one comes off I put on another.7

Goodbye, yours for all ages, affectionate M.; and you ever my dearest and most beloved daughter-sister above all others

10. Anna wants you to send her some stockings. Listen, see whether there are any new ones among Augusta's, and if you have a chance send them; if not, write that there are some but you're waiting for an opportunity, and try to string it out.8 I've given her mine for now, so she can manage for a while. Dear Vincenza, the cotton you sent her is too fine; it takes too long to knit and besides it's too dainty for Daughters of Saint Anne. If you had some thicker, even dark, she'd take it; but don't trouble to buy it or send things, for it costs too much and isn't worth it.

11. Goodbye again, yours, yours; keep well, for charity's sake, so we can still work.

12. How it pleases me when you tell me what you've done in the house! Put the postulant9 in the rooms I wrote to you about, which will be for the Noviciate, in a bed with its curtains.

1 Sr. A. Vincenza had absent-mindedly opened a letter of the Mother's enclosed in hers, but realizing it was for Fr Tornatore, without reading it she had hastened to put it in an envelope and explain to the Father what had happened.

2 Those two: the two gilt sofas.

3 Curtains of non-transparent fabric, Sr. A. Vincenza wrote.

4 That person: Fr Tornatore. Had there been a clash? You'll have received mine. The letter is missing, but there is Sr. A. Vincenza's reply (7 April), in which she describes at length her meeting with the Bishop's Vicar, Mgr Francesco

Tammi, to ask him for a letter to send to Rome to obtain Fr Tornatore's readmission to the Institute.

5 Signora Clotilde Iussi helped several girls staying at the Mother House.

6 This is the letter from Vicar Tammi mentioned in note 4 above.

7 a mosca: a blister.

8 Anna Carrega; Sr. A. Augusta Biagini's.

9 The postulant from Rome. Cf. L 237, n. 4.

The postulant will come at the end of the month, and the Mother hopes she will find everything in order. Poss has written complaining that the Sister in charge of the girls is absent; Vincenza is to go there and urge them to behave well. For the Chapel's inauguration she wants the ceremony to go well: spare no expense, invite many Priests. She hopes there are sheets in the wardrobe and that many are brought: she needs them for all the houses.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I received yours yesterday and hear you're unwell; for charity's sake take care of yourself; write to me, for I'm worried; I'm better and we'll soon see each other.

2. Yes, have the cloth you mention dyed. I'd like it done soon, so that when this postulant comes she may find everything in order: the marble basins, the wardrobes moved and the Novices' beds ready, and put her in one of them; she'll come at the end of the month, leaving with me; I'll stop at Foligno and she'll go on.1

3. Poss wrote complaining that Sr. A. Buon Pastore is in bed, so all the girls seem to be at sixes and sevens. For charity's sake try to go there and urge the girls to be good; if you think more Religious are needed, go ahead, I'm content, as long as it goes well.2

4. I want the ceremony to be done without any stinting: breakfast for the Vicar, and the two F. for the servers and clerics. Tell Don Piacenza to spare nothing, for whatever is needed will be paid. I'd like there to be many Priests; invite the Superior of S. Lazzaro. Make sure there are Priests: our Canon and whoever you think.3

5. I hear about the butcher; how dreadful! Let's hope in God; we'll have everything; I can't wait to hear about the letter sent.4

6. As for the harmonium, you answered well; stick to it that it's too big and always gets damaged when moved, and that he'll do us a great favour by lending his; tell him that if he thinks maestro Volpi should be engaged, you'll engage him. Mind you decorate the Chapel well. As for the pyx, you can ask Don Piacenza to buy you one,5 you know, one of the composite ones I know they have in Piacenza; or else I'll write — never mind, I'll write to Sr. A.
