Santina to send you one, so there'll be no more muddle. What is that person doing — has he been to the Vicar?

7. You tell me there's no more room in the wardrobe for cloth; I'd be only too happy if it were full, but I fear it's [full] on only two shelves and the other two hold the sheets, of which I hope there's a good number. If it were so, let it fill up; then you could put the sheets in the one where the postulants' dresses are and fold those all into a chest, which will be better. Ah, would to God lots of sheets came, for I need them for all the houses. See, my dear, for charity's sake don't pass them on to the girls.6

8. Take care of yourself; write at once to tell me how you are. Goodbye,

yours for ever,

Affectionate [MADRE ROSA]

9. This is the third time I've taken this up again. I write as I talk.

Goodbye, my dear; be cheerful, for charity's sake; please tell the Superior at the Morte to be at peace and that there's nothing wrong;

patience is needed.7

1 This Postulant, cf. L 237, n. 4.

2 Sr. A. del Buon Pastore Dosi was in bed. Someone was needed to replace her,

and other Sisters too.

3 The inauguration ceremony for the Poss factory chapel was to be held on Low Sunday, 12 April. On 7 April Sr. A. Vincenza had asked her for clarifications and all the permissions. The Mother replies in detail. The two F.

(francs) to be given to the two clerics and the master of ceremonies. The Superior of S. Lazzaro, i.e. of the Alberoni College. Our Canon: no further information about him.

4 I hear about the butcher: he had surely complained about late payment. On 13 April Sr. A. Vincenza writes: "Pastore (Sr. A. Buon Pastore) told me there's a debt of Fr. 400 and the miller won't give us flour; for now I have only a few francs." But the Mother does not lose trust in God, either for providence or for Fr Tornatore's readmission to the Institute. That is what she refers to here: I can't wait to hear about the letter sent. It is the request from Bishop Ranza obtained by Sr. A. Vincenza. Cf. L 241, n. 4 and below, par. 6: has that Person been to the Vicar?

5 As for the harmonium. Sr. A. Vincenza's letter is missing and it cannot be learned from any other source what was said, and by whom, about the harmonium for the inauguration of the chapel. Don Pietro Piacenza, chaplain of the Mother House.

6 You tell me there's no more room in the wardrobe for the linen cloth; I'd be only too happy if it were full. The Mother thinks there is no room only on two shelves. She suggests anyway how to remedy it. Don't pass them to the girls: the linen belonged to the Community, having been brought for the most part by postulants who had joined the Institute.

7 The Superior of the Community in Via della Morte: Sr. A. Filippina Bruschi.

As for the Chaplain for the Sampierdarena Community, she should speak with Don Accinelli; the Mother proposes a plan: he could be lodged in a room in the tenant farmer's house and take meals in the Sisters' house. After the clothing she is to send two novices to Genoa, and the others must leave. When Don Accinelli comes to Rome the Mother can settle the matter of the Chaplain with him.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Today I received your letter, so dear to me; the good news you give me is a relief amid so many bitter things [all] day long; my breathing still isn't free; I can't understand it, though I always keep the blisters open; nothing helps. Enough, I hope I'll recover when I leave.1

2. As for the priest, you'd do well to speak with Don Accinelli, as this is a very delicate matter, requiring careful enquiries; I don't know where they could put him; anyway, I want it arranged; another 100 F. or so could be added for lodging, so he wouldn't always be a cross for the nuns.2 Tell Don Accinelli, to whom I'm writing now. If it could be arranged it would be good all round; see what you can do.

3. I hear the seven postulants are being clothed; I hope all goes well; the teacher, in strict confidence, is to serve me for the new house we're going to open in Perugia; silence, for charity's sake; in a few days the one for Sestri will reach you; you'll see her; she seems well suited to me.3

4. Otherwise everything you're doing is fine; you say in one of your letters you want to laugh; as I write, what I had to tell you comes back (to) mind; it's really odd, my dear, when one has to deal with certain creatures who make my head spin; you understand me, don't you? My head can't take it, from every side.4

5. Now, once those 7 are clothed, you'll send them to Genoa; try to leave only (che) the two teachers there and send all the others away, for that house carries too heavy a burden. Ah, when will the holy Mother think of relieving us of those two heartless ones? Enough; I hope the good God will see to it.5

6. Please try to settle the matter of the Priest, if possible; I'd prefer him not to sleep there; eat, yes, but sleep, no. Since at the end of the Villa there's the tenant farmer's house, which is big, perhaps a room could be fitted up there, giving the farmer the ground floor where the brothers still keep timber, and making one upstairs for the Priest with a separate little staircase. What do you think of my plan?6

7. Let Don Accinelli know of it, but without showing him the letter; indeed try to tell him that if you can help in any way he should tell you and you'll do it. Meanwhile hurry things along and try to visit the place together, so you could very well settle things with the Priest, and at last all the gossip would end; and since Don Accinelli comes to Rome on Monday, on his return — so he could tell the Priest — everything would be settled.7

Goodbye, my dear daughter; the Lord give you peace of heart; and always, for all ages, your affectionate M.

1 Sr. A. Francesca's letter has not survived. My breathing...

cf. L 241,9.

2 As for the priest to be engaged as chaplain at the Sampierdarena Institute: she doesn't know where they could put him, i.e. lodge him; the cost of lodging outside could be reckoned, so he would not be a burden (cross) to the Sisters.

3 House in Perugia: cf. L 241,7. The one: the teacher for Sestri.

4 troubles and worries on every side.

5 too heavy a burden, maintaining so many people: ...the two heartless ones, the Vernengo Sisters. Every day they showed little love for the Community by their demands. Cf. L 206, n. 5.

6 Since at the end of the villa: a solution for lodging the Priest occurs to her.

7 hurry things along: try to speed it up. Accinelli is coming to Rome to attend

Anna Carrega's clothing. (Cf. L 209,5).

The postulant can be admitted only on two conditions: that she give up the tobacco habit and submit to a period of probation at the Mother House. As for the other one sent to Piacenza, the Mother points out that she did not keep to what had been laid down about the fee to be paid.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. A line to answer your letter and also the request of the postulant you have with you. With the tobacco habit she can't be admitted; it's forbidden by our Rules; secondly, she would have to go and make her postulancy in Piacenza, since it has been decided that no one may be clothed unless first well tested at the Mother House: they must give sure proof of obedience, vocation and submission.1

2. If she submits to all this, let her find the money for the journey and go to Piacenza with a letter from you — provided she gives up tobacco.

3. I was taken aback by the old woman you sent to Piacenza with so little, when you'd written she'd have much more. It's done now, but don't let it happen again, for so old and with nothing... They're just furniture cluttering our poor house.2

4. I, thanks [to] God, am a little better and trust in your prayers to obtain all I desire for the work. Goodbye, your

Affectionate M.

1 The postulant claimed she took snuff as a medicine.

2 of the old postulant (cf. L 225,1 and 240,1): contrary to what she had previously claimed, she had brought very little money (the two postulants together had given L. 187). Furniture: i.e. encumbrances for our poor house.

She did not write sooner because she was waiting for the Bishop's reply about the two Sisters she wanted to send. Carlotta is to visit the Bishop to find out whether the proposal displeased him. The Mother hopes to be in Pennabilli in mid-May.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Some days ago I received yours together with one from Sr. A. Adelaide; I was slow to reply because I was waiting for a letter from the Bishop answering one I'd written telling him that if it's because of the journey that they don't call the Sisters, I would pay for it. What do you think? Perhaps the Bishop didn't (le) like this? Listen, go and pay him a visit and find out a little.1

2. I hope to be with you by mid-May, so we can settle everything properly in person and spend a little time together.

3. My dear daughter, courage, for great is the crown the good God has prepared for you if you always persevere as you do.

Greet everyone for me. I wish them a thousand blessings from heaven, while you, my beloved daughter, I hug tightly, remaining for ever your affectionate M. R.

1 Sr. A. Carlotta replies to this letter on 19.4. She has been to the Bishop. He is "very troubled at not having been able to answer you... he did all he could with the President too, but could obtain nothing". As for the two Sisters, the President reserves the decision until he speaks with her. For the two Sisters cf. L 191,2; 175, n. 6.

She approves all Vincenza has planned and done to arrange the rooms. To increase the number of girls working at Poss she can approach various people. The Mother is troubled about the cash dowry postulants must bring: if little is asked, or they are accepted free, how can they be maintained? She asks about the dormitories and suggests some additions.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I've just received yours and am replying; I hope you've received mine urging you to speak to that person so that he wouldn't stir a straw; if he hasn't done it, let him not do it now; he should have gone earlier.1

2. You did well about the sheets; for charity's sake see that all who come bring at least a good quantity, so we can build up a large stock; for you know I've accepted another house in Perugia and I have to provide all the linen; so see to it, my dear.2

3. I'm glad to hear all the work is finished; now I'm waiting to hear the upstairs is done; as they finish the rooms, put them in order, so they'll be ready for the postulants at once.

4. We'll find the girls I promised Poss here and there; I think the Parish Priest of the Paganina still has some; look into it; I hear you've taken two more, so that'll be 18, not twenty. If Accinelli has some, you can write asking him to send them, or tell Sr. A. Francesca. Listen, send her a portrait, poor thing; I'm writing to her now.3

5. How it grieves me to hear we could have had money for that postulant and instead only 200 F. How dreadful! My dear, God knows how much we need; stand firm when they come with that line; tell them: "we can't!" He won't have thought of it; and hold firm at F. 500.4 I've accepted another one here, but for F. 800, if she comes. I hope you'll do it; so if he said it, we say so too; it certainly is a serious matter. Who pays the three hundred francs for meat? and we can never put a cent together. How this house grieves me, the more so now that there are more mouths.5

6. Find out what the baths are called that Mother Landi goes to every year; she'd like to know what they're good for. If you see Albertazzi you can ask him. Listen, it occurs to me that Albertazzi is owed F. 200 for 1873.6

7. And you can't imagine how the chemist's bill worries me; never mind the Marchioness!7 My dear, if we wait for help from her, I think the Daughters of Saint Anne would starve. Isn't that so, my Vincenza?

8. If you thought of making a trip to Cortemaggiore to fetch the postulant before I send the one from Rome, you wouldn't have to move again; meanwhile you'd pay; between the two you'd settle all the bills.8

9. I've started praying again for that house, and I hope the funds will reach you and you'll soon write to tell me.

10. How is your room? And is ours finished? When will you clothe the ones I wrote to you about? And when are you putting Cecilia at the end of the Novices' dormitory?9 But I'd like her not to make a mess; keep it clean.

11. Have you had any iron frames made for the beds in the girls' dormitory that's closed? What would you say if we managed to put frames on every other bed, with curtains: what luxury! Then girls of every kind could go there, couldn't they?10

12. But if postulants keep coming with nothing, it's dreadful! Expenses on every side and never any income! I commend the sheets to you.

13. Now the things you want to send: I'd say send nothing; they'd like salami, but what can I say, transport costs too much, and for so few days; it seems a waste of money. Goodbye, yours for an eternity.

Affectionate M.

14. P.S. Silence: on Monday that person takes the veil; pray and have others pray; tell that person; it's a tremendous business.11

1 The letter the Mother is answering is missing. Mine: L 242,6, where she writes:

has that person been to the Vicar? It was a matter of urging him to send to Rome a letter for Fr Tornatore's readmission to the Institute. Cf. L 241, n. 4.

2 another house in Perugia, cf. L 241,7; 243,3.

3 the girls I promised Poss. She had committed herself to a certain number, but they had fallen short, because six girls from Nizza had left the factory and gone home. Others must be found: ask the Parish Priest Don Elia Magnani, Don Accinelli, Sr. A. Francesca Camisa. She urges her to send the last-named a photograph of herself. The photos were a gift from Countess Trotti. Cf. letter of

Rapallino to M. Rosa 9.4.1874.

4 What the Mother says is not entirely clear. Perhaps Fr Tornatore had told someone the Institute accepted postulants who brought F. 500

or even less.

5 How it grieves me. The Mother House, now that mouths have increased with the arrival of postulants, causes her worry.

6 They are the sulphur baths of Tabiano, Sr. A. Vincenza replies on 21 April.

She notes that the Community doctor Sante Albertazzi is owed

F. 200 for 1873.

7 The Chemist was owed F. 1,542. They had fondly imagined that this bill would be settled by Marchioness Fanny Anguissola.

8 A piece of advice. With the fees of the postulant from Cortemaggiore and the one from Rome she could have paid off all the debts.

9 Cecilia: Sr. A. Cecilia Tortini.

10 iron frame (trappa): a framework fitted to the bed to hang curtains round it.

11 Anna Carrega is the person taking the veil of the Daughters of Saint Anne. She is to inform Fr Tornatore. It is a tremendous business, as the Marquis her Father obstinately refused his consent.

She tells her that Anna's Clothing will take place the next day. Don Gaetano has written wanting to be paid by Don Biale; Vincenza is to speak to Don Biale and urge him to pay his debts, borrowing from Don Accinelli. She asks for some information and urges her to look after her health and live in peace.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Read this letter to C. and then give it to Mr T. to read; imagine, you know I never had any thought of accepting such creatures; nor does Mr Poss want them, you know, because they're lazy. Enough; Piacenza always has something new. Now I'm writing to Poss and to the Bishop so that he can answer these most worthy Sisters.1

2. My dear, tomorrow Anna's clothing takes place. Imagine what battles (che) will arise, but let's pay no heed; courage; until death we'll cry: "Long live Jesus!"2 I can't wait to leave Rome. I'm tired; I hope you've received my letter.

3. Listen: Don Gaetano writes that he wants to be paid by Don Biale; do me the kindness of going there and telling him, for charity's sake, to pay these people, and the doctor too; let him write to Don Accinelli to lend him the money, but let him pay. If he writes like that, Accinelli will send it; so let him not put it off any longer.3

4. Ah, I'd also like you to be able to pay the doctor for 1873.4 Let's hope the Lord sends you the money. My expenses here are an abyss.

5. When you see my dear postulant, I'm sure you'll be pleased.5 Today I thought I'd get letters from you, lazybones! I write to you every day. Tomorrow is the great ceremony.

6. And then that person hasn't gone again to commend himself? What patience! My dear, everything falls on the one with the flayed back: everything on me!6

7. When convenient, I'd like you to write and tell me how many sheets there are — you know, only those belonging strictly to the community, not those the postulants brought; forgive my curiosity; it will guide me when I ask you for some.

8. For charity's sake don't overtire yourself; take care; do what you do in peace; keep after the gardener too, so he works the garden well and puts it in good order.

9. Tell me, do you know anything more about the Marchioness?7 They've written to me that all is at peace. Blessed be the Lord!

10. Goodbye, for I still have so much to write. Your affectionate M.

for ever, and always near, to enjoy the sufferings we have borne. Yes, my dear, what consolation! we'll laugh at everyone and live with Jesus for eternity. Long live suffering!8

your Affectionate M. R.

1 Neither the content of the letter nor the addressee can be determined.

2 At last, Sr. A. Carrega's clothing. The sense in which the Mother uses the word battles is not clear. Perhaps the opposition of a brother of

Carrega's who was in Rome.

3 Don Gaetano Bersani and the doctor wanted to be paid by Don Biale

(cf. L 142,5).

4 Pay the doctor: cf. L 246, n. 6.

5 My dear postulant, cf. L 237, n. 4.

6 That person: Fr Tornatore was to commend himself; to whom, we cannot know.

7 Marchioness Fanny Anguissola, cf. L 100, n. 10.

8 Suffering makes us long for, and prepares us for, eternal joy, where no one can make us suffer any more; we shall live with Jesus for ever.

She thanks her for what she sent through Alessandro. Her news of the house is a joy, but even more what she says about keeping the Rules. She is glad they are at last in a bigger house. She urges them to love the Lord; in pleasing him one is happy and gives true witness.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Forgive me for not writing as soon as I received the decoction; it was the great pressure of work. Now I'm with you to say how welcome the decoction was and how much good it did me; one bottle broke, a pity;1 there was a big stone in the basket, it must have been that; thank you also for the orange-flower water.

2. My daughter, how your letters please me, always bringing such consoling news of providence and of the house;2 but what pleases me most is when you tell me the Rules are kept, and when I hear you have many sick people.

3. Now that the house is bigger I'll send you nurses, so you can do more nursing without wearing yourselves out; that's my wish.3

4. Courage, my daughter, and pray for me, for the tribulations are immense; I desire nothing but to bear them with resignation and as my God wills! Yes, my dear, when I can be sure that what I do and suffer pleases my Jesus, I am happy; so I hope of you and the others that your happiness will be nothing other than pleasing the Lord.4

Yes! once we have attained this, my dears, we want nothing more.

5. Enough! enough! Love dear Jesus very much and then be cheerful, so as to make everyone want to follow you in the apostolate of converting souls.5 Courage, for one day we shall rest for eternity.

Your Affectionate M. God bless you all. Pray, pray!

1 Cf. L 239, n. 2.

2 news... of the house, cf. L 239, n. 3.

3 The sick wanting to be nursed by the Sisters were always numerous.

4 your happiness... pleasing the Lord. This sums up her trinitarian spirituality: guided by the Spirit, with Jesus and in Jesus, to be the delight of the

Father.

5 Love and be cheerful: to witness by one's life how beautiful and joyful it is to live for Jesus is the most effective apostolate for attracting souls.

From the Parrocchietta she gives the good news of Anna Carrega's Clothing; she is now Sr. A. Benedetta. She suggests Francesca advise Sr. A. Santina to send her some money. She wants the Sisters to lack nothing: they work and need enough food. She is to do her best to have the Communities follow the Spiritual Exercises preached by Fr Defilippi.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I'm at the Parrocchietta and, having a little time, I'm giving part of it to you, my dear, whom I always keep with me wherever I go. Do you know why I'm here? enough, I'll tell you in person, for fear this gets lost.

2. Now I've good news for you: Anna is ours; since yesterday (che) she's been called Sr. A. Benedetta. Silence, silence, for charity's sake!1

3. I hope they'll bring me letters from you today, but I'm going down at once, not stopping, and I hope (che) to leave early in May; you know we've opened another house in Perugia.2

4. Listen, now that Don Accinelli is away, I'd like you (che) to tell Sr. A. Santina — as if from yourself — to set aside the money she receives and then send it to me, I mean a month's worth, after expenses, and to pay for the flour herself, so she gets used to managing on her own. What do you think? Listen, I'm suggesting this, but do it only if you think fit. Think it over and then do as you judge best. I don't say they should give him nothing, but a third, which would be somewhat more than the rent;3 tell her to feed the Sisters well, and that the bread be good. That's my wish. Since providence is coming in there, let them lack nothing; waste, no — against the dear jewel of poverty, no — but too little and poor food, no either, for they work very hard.4

5. I hope you've seen to the Chapel. I can't wait to hear you announce it.5 I hope Defilippi will also give the Exercises at S. P. d'Arena in the house, and then to you in the hospital; do them as best you can; that's my wish; and at Sestri too; make the most of it. At Sestri see that they prepare a nicely arranged room for him, and let him go there too, so I won't have to think about it for a year.6

6. I rely on you. I very much hope he'll take those two vipers in hand and straighten out their heads; it would be a first-class miracle. I'm writing him a couple of lines now to encourage him to do what is so badly needed.7

7. Have you perhaps had Carlotta's dress made? Then you could send it to her, for she'd take off her heavy wool, as it's already warm.8

8. I hope you've thought about the Priest and received my letter.9 This time I hope you won't complain that I write too little. I'm always in credit. Ah, my dear Francesca, one day indeed we shall no longer need to write or long for news of each other, but held close together we shall be with our Good, to enjoy him for eternity. Then all our pains will seem little to us, seeing that they alone brought us a great good. Courage! Long live the cross with suffering! Long may it live!10

Yours for ever, affectionate M. R.

1 Anna Carrega, now Sr. A. Benedetta. Silence. The news must not be spread, since the Marquis her Father opposes his daughter's decision.

2 I'm going down: back to Rome. We've opened another house in Perugia: that of S. Martinello. Cf. L 241,7; 243,3; 246,2.

3 Now he's away: Don Accinelli was in Rome. He managed the

Genoa house, and the Superior Santina handed him the surplus money.

Now the Mother wants the Superior to get used to managing herself, but leaves it to the discretion of Sr. A. Francesca. I don't say they should give nothing to Don Accinelli, but a third of the surplus, so that he can pay the rent and some other expenses.

4 Let her feed them well... for they work very hard. Cf. L 135,6; 136,5; 138, n. 7; 175,6.

For the hospital Chapel she was to invite the Archbishop to bless it. Cf. L 207, n. 4.

5 For the hospital chapel she was to invite the Archbishop to bless it. Cf. L 207, n. 4.

6 Giuseppe Defilippi was to preach the Spiritual Exercises to the Community.

Cf. L 206,9.

7 I hope he'll take in hand: that he'll manage to bring the two Vernengo sisters to reason. Cf. L 206, n. 5.

8 Carlotta's dress; the Mother had asked her for it. Cf. L 218,5.

9 the priest: the chaplain for the Sampierdarena House. Cf. L 243,2,6,7.

10 To her dear daughter, who longs to have her near, she opens the vision of an inexpressible joy, free of anxiety and waiting, the fulfilment of a joy unattainable on earth — a joy all the more intense the more numerous the sufferings have been. Courage! Forward with zeal under the banner of the cross.

Rome: Chapel of the Oblates of Tor de' Specchi, where Sr. A. Benedetta Carrega received the habit of the Daughters of Saint Anne.

Thinking again about what she advised in the previous letter, she asks her not to speak to the Superior Santina about the financial matter in question.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. A line in haste to tell you that for charity's sake you must say nothing to Sr. A. Santina, for it would be a serious matter; if you've already spoken to her, try to go there and put it right, telling her to take no notice whatever of what you said.2

2. Sleep is overcoming me; it's late and today I'm very tired. You can imagine I have Don Accinelli with me.3 Enough, I'm going to sleep. I'll tell you everything in person.

I am your affectionate MADRE

1 This letter was sent after the previous one (cf. L 249).

2 Contrary to what she had advised her to suggest to the Superior Santina, after speaking with Don Accinelli she has understood that it is better not to change anything (cf. L 249,4).

3 He had come to Rome for Anna Carrega's clothing.

She is to keep the sick girl at the Mother House. She is to clothe the postulants, but after the Spiritual Exercises. She is to finish the work on the house and pay the debts. The Mother longs to leave Rome.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I haven't written for two days because of the heavy work that doesn't leave me a minute. In your last you told me Sireni is ill; for pity's sake don't send her there again; take her home with you.1

2. You told me you have postulants to clothe; I say yes, but first I'd like them to make at least 5 days' retreat; then clothe them as soon as you can, for they're needed.

3. I hope the builders will soon finish upstairs; while they're there, we'll have to do the laundry. Did you have the corridor shutters cleaned, which you said needed it — I don't remember — and I wrote yes? Be quick and pay all the bills, for charity's sake, so they can't say anything more.

4. Go and see Marchioness Anguissola; if only the Lord would touch her heart!2

5. Yesterday I went to the Pope and had a private audience. What fine things he said to me! Next Thursday we're going to the Fornaci with Mgr Negrotto, and then, if they finish the Father's business, I'll leave at once.3

6. I'm waiting for letters from you; that person must be always asleep, for he no longer writes.4 I can't wait to leave. My health is good; I get up early, I work — crippled, yes, but always on my feet. God be blessed! I owe it all to my Rosa, dear holy creature.5 [Nothing] more for now, as I have to go out. Yours for ever,

affectionate M. R.

1 Giuseppa Sereni was an orphan girl taken into the Mother House in 1869.

2 Marchioness Anguissola. Cf. L 100, n. 10.

3 To the Fornaci with Mgr Augusto Negrotto to visit the School. The Father's business: Fr Tornatore's readmission, for which the intervention of the Bishop of Piacenza, Mgr Ranza, had also been sought through his Vicar. Cf. L 241,

n. 4; 242, n. 4.

4 Fr Tornatore.

5 My Rosa Parodi, the dear friend who died in the odour of sanctity, to whom she prayed with confidence and whose powerful intercession she felt. Cf. L 178, n. 1.

She outlines her travel plans. Notes on the postulants and their accommodation. Vincenza is to send Carlotta, who will travel with Don Accinelli, her half-mourning dress.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I've just finished reading your letter about D. Giovanni. You did well in what you write; now D. Accinelli will come and give him what he deserves; meanwhile be patient.1

2. As for the postulants, for charity's sake clothe as many as you can, lots of them, for I need them desperately. Instead of one from Rome I'm sending you 2, very good ones. On Saturday I leave for Foligno, where I'll stay 5 or 6 days, then Perugia for 2 days, then Pennabilli, Bologna, Ferrara and Piacenza at last.

3. Please see to the washbasins; rest assured I'll be pleased with whatever you've done.2

4. Put the postulant who's coming with the young Lady — she too is a young lady — wherever you think best, as long as it's suitable and clean. As for the lame postulant, you can tell him to send her for you to see, and if you can take her, take her. The other two, if they're strong, accept them, for charity's sake, even with F. 100, simply because I need them; and as you clothe those you have, others will come at once. It stays always full.3

5. Now listen: you told me you've had iron frames4 fitted to four of the girls' beds in the big dormitory; well done; but I'd also like you to arrange these four beds like this: right at the top by the door one with curtains, then one without, then one with curtains and one without — that's four; you have two left over, so put them on the other side as you come in, one with and one without, and in the curtained ones you can put the young ladies. All right? That's for when you have no more room to put them. What do you think? For washing, let them always go where the girls used to go. Since they're nuns, I think they'll be able to keep it clean there, and they could draw water from the well, putting on top, if you think fit, that container with a tap that was in the girls' kitchen; it could be set a little into the wall and fixed. What do you think? It would look good in marble, but for now we must economize; in due course; meanwhile they could keep this one always full, and so they'd all wash there.

6. Try to have a few pictures made to put in

those rooms the builders are fixing up. I hear you have no money; I hope that today St Joseph, it being his Patronage, will have sent you some.5 Goodbye, yours for all ages,

M. affectionate

7. Carlotta asks you to send her the half-mourning dress she has in the wardrobe, last year's grey one, because she needs it for the journey right away. She's staying in Rome while I go to Foligno. Don Accinelli will bring it to me;6 send it at once; it will arrive in time; don't delay a moment once you've received this. Send me nothing else. Goodbye; everyone sends greetings.

8. As for bread, you can give it to the girls with a little slice of fat bacon, and they'd be happy.7

2 On the washbasins, cf. L 234,13.

3 The postulant coming with the young lady: the two from Rome. The lame postulant, you can tell him: she had been put forward by the Vicar of Soresina together with the other two.

4 the frames (frappe), cf. L 246, n. 10.

5 That day was the feast of the "Patronage of St Joseph".

6 Don Accinelli, on his way back to Genoa, was to stop in Piacenza. Cf. L

250, n. 3.

7 Sr. A. Vincenza had asked whether the girls working at the

Poss factory could have bread in the morning "instead of polenta; so, making a soup, they could put the bit of bread left over in their pockets and eat it at the factory".

She gives instructions about the Sister nurses attending Signora Airenta.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. A line to tell you to go and visit Signora Airenta at S. P. d'Arena1 and tell her that if she needs nurses I've written to you to send her two for a week, and after that week they'll be changed for another two.

2. They'll stay there day and night and eat what the Lady gives them — you know, two dishes and soup and a piece of fruit; do it at once. Send Emanuela and one of the most recently clothed;2 for the next week send another two. I'm writing to Piacenza to send you two at once.

Goodbye, in haste, your

Affectionate M.

2 Sr. A. Emanuela Zumi, older in vocation.

She has told the Superiors to send the post to Piacenza. Until the 7th she will be in Foligno and will tell her where and when to forward it. She has had a letter from the Father and is pleased with what has been done at the Poss factory. She has obtained the Holy Father's blessing for it.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. For your guidance: on Saturday, God willing, I leave for Foligno; if you receive letters from other Superiors — as I've written to them all to send them to you there — you'll always know my movements. 2. Nothing new about that person; where is he? In ecstasy perhaps? I know nothing more; it's nearly a fortnight since I heard anything.2 And what are you doing? I'm expecting letters from you today. For charity's sake take care of yourself.

3. When Don Accinelli comes, I hope he'll find the [postulants] clothed; I'd be inclined to wait before handing the teacher over to him; meanwhile she gains more experience, and the others too.3

4. Poss wants a Superior. Do you know who came to mind? Sr. A. Angiola; she's deaf, as it happens, and won't suffer from the noise. What do you think? Think it over.4

6. The Holy Father blessed this factory with a rescript of his containing very beautiful words.7 I commend this factory to you. Goodbye; be cheerful, for we'll soon see each other. At last I'm setting sail from Rome; your affectionate

M. R.

2 She has no news of Fr Tornatore.

My daughter,

1. A line in haste to tell you I leave Rome on Saturday 2 May. Address your letters to Piacenza, where they have orders to forward them to me wherever I am.1

2. I've received yours and heard all about the Countess, and about the Schools.2

3. Have prayers said that I may have a good journey, for it's very long and tiring; pray to the most blessed Virgin that nothing may happen to me and that I may arrive safely.

Goodbye; greet everyone for me. God bless you, and believe me your affectionate M. ROSA

She has received her letter. She will write later to let her know where she is. Vincenza is to write the address and hand letters to the postman. Her letter brought consolation with the news that every debt is paid. She commends to her the two postulants arriving from Rome.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Yesterday I received your letter and two lines from that person. I will write as soon as I arrive to give you news of the journey; and pr[ay] and have prayers said that I may travel safely, and all the rest.

Goodbye, in haste, your

affec[tionate]

She received her letter a few hours ago and leaves for Foligno today. She has explained to D. Accinelli what Vincenza wanted to know about the work. She is pleased with what she is doing; she should not worry about the girls: they will recover.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Just a line to tell you I received yours a few hours ago, today, Friday; tomorrow I leave for Foligno, where, God willing, I'll arrive at midday; write to me there.

2. I've told Don Accinelli everything about the washbasin;2 as for the old woman, I say absolutely not, because it would mean taking on a chronic invalid; answer no.3 Otherwise I'm delighted with what you're doing; don't worry about the girls' illness.4 Ask Poss to let them stay in bed longer in the morning, and then make a novena to the Eternal Father; you'll see they'll recover. Goodbye, for I have no time; yours. Goodbye, your

Affectionate M. ROSA

She thanks her for the money order and asks for prayers.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I've received your letter with the money order inside. Thank you for remembering and for your good heart towards your poor mother; I didn't write sooner because I received it the very moment I was leaving,2 and then on arrival you know how busy I am.

2. Tell the Sisters to pray hard for the journey I have to make,3 and that I may complete all I told them before leaving. Goodbye, for I'm in a hurry; your

Affectionate Mother

1 It was classified as dated 6 April 1874, from Rome. The content shows it to be from May and therefore from Foligno.

2 She had left Rome on 2 May. Cf. L 256,2.

3 the journey: cf. L 252,2. But she later changed her plans for health reasons. Cf. L 259.

She warmly urges observance, without which the service of charity is reduced to mere human labour, lacking the foundation of faith and charity. She is unwell and longs to be with her daughters. She hopes to see her again in Piacenza. Francesca is to look after herself and get treatment.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I've received your long letter telling me so much about observance.1 My daughter, listen: if you don't see to it that it is kept, everything else will go from bad to worse. Observance is the pivot of our actions; without it we can do no good; laxity sets in, harmony among the Sisters vanishes, grumbling becomes the main business of the day, and worse, certain ugly things follow which are the ruin of communities. Observance is the sweet bond of perfection, which helps us one another to run along that dear path of peace and union.2

2. For pity's sake, try to put things in order, otherwise it's merely human labour and will end with the fall of our life; let us build on solid ground, not on sand, so that our buildings may last for eternity.3

3. Those two Sisters, so stubborn and proud — punish them without pity; death is better than living out of God's grace; pride is abhorred by Jesus, so whoever is proud is sure to be abhorred by the Lord and can expect nothing but eternal death.4

4. Listen, I hope to be in Piacenza on Saturday, because I don't feel well, so I'm hurrying the journey out of fear. Today I'm breathing better, but yesterday I had to apply a blister; I can't wait to be in your arms. How I miss you! Well, you spoiled me, so it's hard to be away from you. I remember all the things you did for me. Ah, you spoiled me far too much!5

5. Enough; see whether you can arrange with the director to have two days' leave: I'd telegraph you, but I don't know how. What can I say, at stations I have to do everything myself, so — what a trial — I feel ill having to do one thing after another; I don't know whether I'll manage. Anyway, you know, don't you? So unless you have some objection, on Saturday next week I'll be in Piacenza. Goodbye. Take care of yourself, for charity's sake; look after your health, for once lost it can't be regained. Goodbye, for my side hurts. God bless you with the others; your affectionate M. R. I leave here on Monday, the day after tomorrow.6

1 Sr. A. Francesca's letter is of 2 May. The hospital work certainly kept the Sisters busy full time and made community acts difficult and sometimes impossible.

2 If you don't see to it that it is kept. In a few lines the Mother encapsulates great wisdom. Observance of the Rule is the pivot of action because it fills it with charity towards God and the sick. Observance attunes the Sisters to one rhythm and is a source of peace, harmony and mutual agreement, leading all to unity.

3 The conclusion is full of the Gospel spirit: build on rock, not on sand, otherwise our life will be fruitless in time and in eternity.

Cf. Matt 7:24-27.

4 Those two stubborn and proud Sisters. They must be corrected for their own good. The proud person runs not on the way towards Jesus but on the way away from him, the way of death.

5 to be there on Saturday. Instead she went to Rimini. Cf. L 261. I can't wait: a frank and spontaneous outpouring of affectionate gratitude and tenderness towards the Daughters who had surrounded her with attention and tenderness.

6 I leave here on Monday the 11th. She actually left on Wednesday the 13th.

My daughter,

1. I add a line to tell you I may not leave Foligno tomorrow, Monday, after all, but am putting it off until Wednesday the 13th, and I'll stop at Frimino for two or three days and then in Bologna.1 I fear I shan't be in Piacenza on Saturday. I'd better telegraph you when I leave Bologna, so you'll know my arrival in Piacenza more surely.

Goodbye; I'm sorry to hear you haven't received letters from me; it means they're getting lost. Patience!

Goodbye, your affectionate M.

My daughter,

My daughter,

1. Yesterday I received your letter about the Bishop and the postulant. I'm always ready at a word from you to send you the Sister, and then you can send the other one here.1

2. Courage, for that alone can sustain us; and observance is the anchor that holds us fast in the harbour of our vocation; without it we shall never do well.2 I won't dwell on this, for I know how attached and steadfast you are in it. Rather a thousand deaths, my beloved daughter, than fail.

Give my regards to Sr. A. Adelaide and Sr. A. Dorotea,3 and receive a close embrace in the heart of Jesus, while

I remain your affectionate M. R.

1 A girl wanted to enter the Institute. At her meeting with the Superior

Biagini in Rimini, she had agreed to transfer a Sister.

3 Sr. A. Adelaide Cervini and Sr. A. Dorotea Benedetti.

She urges her to receive visitors well, acting in her place.

A.M.F.

Dear daughter,

1. A word to tell you that if any visitors come, whoever they may be, try to give everyone a warm welcome.1 You know why I write this — I'd forgotten;2 act as if you were me, and besides you're in your own house. I'll say no more.

Yours for all ages, affectionate MADRE ROSA

1 Sr. A. Benedetta is now at the Mother House. M. Rosa, away for a short time, gives her a task of great importance.

2 I'd forgotten. She probably had in mind someone who was going to call.

She will arrive in Piacenza in a day and will tell her many things.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. A line to you too, my dear; it seems an age since I saw you.2 Tomorrow I'll be with you and tell you lots of things in person. Meanwhile let us hold close to our God, so as to be with him for eternity.

Goodbye, mine for all ages.

[MADRE ROSA]

2 it seems an age. This expression, like those that follow, reveals strikingly the quality of the relationship between M. Rosa and this daughter of her heart,

She has just returned from Milan. She awaits letters with further explanations about the Sestri and Sampierdarena houses.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Here I am back from Milan, and at once I'm giving you my news, which, thank the Lord, is good. I received yours before leaving. I'd have liked to write to you, but you can certainly imagine whether I could.

2. The Superior at Sestri wrote that the Municipality has given her F. 360 for the rent of the house she is leaving.1 I'm waiting for letters from you describing things better; (is it) the old woman who wants to write to Fr Santi? Mind, I don't want that; listen to her, and then, if she wants to write to a lawyer, let her write the letter and send it to me (me); then I'll see it, and if I think it right to send it I will; otherwise I'll keep it.2

3. I'm anxious to hear something from S. P. d'Arena, what we discussed;3 I'll write no more because I'm tired.

Goodbye, dear daughter; believe me for all ages your

Affectionate M.

1 The one at Sestri: Sr. A. Filomena Pugnaloni... for the rent of the house she is leaving. Perhaps the house the Sisters were leaving for another.

2 The old woman. There is not enough information to identify her. From the text she seems a postulant presented by Fr Baldassare Santi SJ, who, having affairs to settle,

wanted to entrust the matter to him.

She thanks her for her prayers, which she sorely needs. She too prays the Lord for holiness, light and the virtues a Superior needs. She is to be always cheerful, as the Mother is, in suffering as in joy.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter C.

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. A line to thank you for the prayers you say and have said for me. Keep it up, my dear, for I sorely need them, first for my soul, since I'm on the edge of the grave and so unprepared; in body I'm very poorly; my head feels as if there were a nail in the middle of my forehead. The rest God knows, our good.

2. I'm very glad of the news in your long letter, which I received today. God reward you; this poor mother of yours can do nothing but raise prayers to the Lord every day, that he may make my daughter a great saint and give her the light she needs to guide her community well.

3. Prudence, meekness and charity: with these three virtues, which I hope God the Father will grant my prayer to give you, you will guide the Daughters of Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate, along the way of perfection.3

4. Away with irritability, away with sulking; always cheerful, in adversity as in fair weather and joy; always the same, in the presence of God the Father, always cheerful.4

5. Amid so many spasms I make everyone laugh and laugh myself, and I want you to do the same. Forgive the bad writing and greet the Sisters; have Sr. A. Carolina pray for me. Goodbye; the Lord bless you all and pour his choicest blessings on you in particular and make you a saint; I am your affectionate MADRE ROSA

1 This letter was classified among the undated ones to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa, but from the tone and content she does not seem to be the addressee. It was surely found among her correspondence. It may be to Sr. A. Augusta Biagini, for some time at Sampierdarena, guided and helped by Francesca in running the community.

2. Given the Mother's request in paragraph 5, "have Sr. A. Carolina pray for me", the letter can be dated to this period, since Sr. A. Carolina had received the habit of the Daughters of Saint Anne at the Sampierdarena Institute on 17 April 1874 (cf. letters of Sr. A. Augusta and Don Accinelli to M. Rosa, of 18 April and 11 April 1874 respectively).

3 These are the three virtues every Superior needs; Sr. A. Augusta needed them greatly, since more than one person considered her a "girl".

4 The second exhortation aims more directly at this Superior's faults.

She has had a letter from Don Tito asking for two more religious; she will send them. Vincenza is to tell the Superior that, as she needs rest, she should go to Sampierdarena and stay a while.

A.M.F.

Dear Vincenza,

1. I couldn't write to you yesterday. Everything went well and I've already settled everything. Blessed be God.

2. Listen, Don Tito wants me to send him more religious, but not the Superior; indeed he'd like me to take her away;1 well then, do this: leave Sr. A. Giacomina as she is, in her post, and bring away Sr. A. Serafina;2 and so on; I'll send him two nurses as I wrote to Don Tito, but you needn't wait for them.

3. Tell the Superior to concentrate on getting well and take care of herself, and that I have no intention of removing her; what I did was purely for her good, so that she might recover.3 If so, all the better.

Goodbye; I'm expecting you; tell Carlotta I'll tell her everything in person. I'm too busy.

Goodbye to all; I can't wait to see you,

your affectionate M. R.

1 Sr. A. Vincenza had gone to Ovada to accompany Sr. A. Serafina

Fantini as the new Superior, but Don Tito Borgatta wrote to the Mother to send two more religious and not the Superior; indeed he wants her to leave.

2 It is therefore prudent to leave Sr. A. Giacomina Schenardi there as Superior.

3 Tell the Superior Giacomina to take care of herself; she had taken that step not to remove her but so that she might recover.

Her letter grieves her with the bad news of her poor health. That's what comes of working so hard and not looking after one's health! She will send a Sister whom Francesca is to train well, so she can leave her as vice-superior and go to Piacenza to rest.

A.M.F.

My Francesca,

1. I've just received your letter and hasten to reply. Alas, you're ill! Listen, did you know I sent Sr. A. Serafina to Ovada to replace the Superior?2 Sr. A. Vincenza writes that she's doing very well and grasps everything the first time. I'm very sorry I didn't send her to you, but I'll do it at once: I'll replace her with another and send her to you with a religious, but you'll put the latter in Genoa and take an older, steadier one for yourself; then train Sr. A. Serafina and present her as vice-Superior to help you.3

2. Let her do whatever you think fit, and little by little she'll end up staying there as Superior, so you can come here and rest.

3. See what you do? After working so hard and refusing to take care of yourself, what happens?4 If I had a moment free I'd come and see you, but I'm alone; Sr. A. Vincenza hasn't come yet, and on Tuesday I must go to Ferrara for 8 days; but before then you'll have your companion, and I hope you'll give me better news.5

4. For pity's sake, have someone write to me every day, even twice a day; today I'm already tempted to telegraph.

5. Thank you for the things you sent; poor child, you think of me, and I can do nothing for you! What suffering! Now at once a new Sister for you, so that you get well quickly and come here.6 I'm so agitated I'd fly to see you. My dear Francesca, for pity's sake look after yourself and get well.7 Yours in haste, affectionate for ever and ever. Amen.

[MADRE ROSA]

1 The date follows from comparison with L 272.

2 She had instead to bring her back. Cf. L 272, n. 1.

3 I'll send her to you... another older in vocation and better formed.

4 ...after working so hard. She had subjected herself to stressful and excessive work, even staying up nights so that the whole hospital might run in good order.

5 Tuesday 9 June.

6 at once a new one: another Sister with you.

7 I'm so agitated... I'd fly... get well. These lively, spontaneous expressions show concern, solicitude, anxiety and distress at not being able to obtain in person what she desires.

She suggests how to correct a Sister. She will send two Sisters to Genoa; Francesca is to take two from that community in exchange. The Mother will need Sr. A. Serafina to replace the Superior at Ovada. Francesca is to find out what is going on between the teacher and the Sister from Sestri and try to correct them, without getting upset. She is to send Sr. A. Giacomina to Piacenza.

A.M.F.

My Francesca,

1. Yesterday your telegram relieved my anxiety, though I hardly believe it.1 Today I received both your letters together; I'll answer what you say about Sr. A. Elvira. You know already: you can tell her to ask the Sisters' pardon in the refectory for three days for the scandal she gave, and then make a novena to the holy Mother to obtain that she never again give such scandal to outsiders. As for Sr. A. Apollonia, do as you say; you know I always approve everything.2

2. Tomorrow I'm sending two to Genoa, and you'll go and choose two you think good. I've written to Don Accinelli and will write to the Superior too. The ones I'm sending don't seem suitable to me; besides, not the young one, for she's contrary and needs a firm hand; the other has no strength. Listen, don't take Sr. A. Geltrude, for I need her myself.3

3. You tell me to keep Sr. A. Serafina for myself — never! I can't wait to be able to send someone to Ovada, for I can no longer send Sr. A. Giacomina there, after her usual muddles at Nizza.4 My dear, so many troubles — you can't imagine.

4. Have a word with the teacher of the house, for she writes that she horrifies the Sisters; look into it; have them come to you, the one from Sestri; don't wear yourself out; have them come to you and scold them, but without harming yourself, for charity's sake.5

5. Look after yourself, for I really feel ill when I hear you're unwell. Do you want to leave me alone in a sea of tribulations?

6. When I write to you to send Sr. A. Giacomina here, do it without her realizing; wait for the time of the train and send her either with postulants or with nuns I'll tell you about, buying her a through ticket to here.6

Goodbye, my dear; I hug you tight and remain your

affectionate MADRE

1 It told her she was better.

2 Sr. A. Francesca's two letters have not survived, so neither the fault of Sr. A. Elvira Persiani nor the decision about Sr.

A. Apollonia Marchetti is known.

3 I'm sending two religious from the last clothing to Genoa, and you'll go and choose two from that community you think best suited to the hospital, because those

I'm sending are not suitable. But don't take Sr. A. Geltrude

Gottelli for the hospital.

4 the usual muddles at Nizza. The Mother had moved her from that house during a visit to the community in September 1872.

5 The teacher of the Sampierdarena house is scandalizing the Sisters; have them come to you and reprove them, but without distressing yourself. The sentence is unclear.

6 When I write to you to send her. Sr. A. Giacomina was at Sampierdarena for a period of rest. Cf. L 272,3. ...without her realizing: so that she doesn't know in advance. When the train (the steamer) leaves, give her the task of accompanying to Piacenza the postulants and nuns I shall indicate.

Two religious are joining her community in exchange for two whom the Superior Francesca will choose for the Hospital. She commends the younger one to her.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. These two religious are coming in exchange for two whom the Superior Francesca will come and choose for the hospital.1

2. I commend young Sr. A. Evangelista to you: always send her accompanied by a Sister old in years and vocation.2 Greet the Sisters for me, and receive a goodbye from your affectionate

Have many prayers said to the Sacred Heart for two graces I desire,

your M. R.

3. Give this paper to Don Accinelli, with my

very, very warm regards.3

1 Cf. L 274,2.

2 The young one: Sr. A. Evangelista Bartoli had received the habit on 5 May

1874. She urges her always to send her to nurse the sick at home accompanied by a Sister old in years and vocation.

She is to persuade the Superior Giacomina not to leave until the Mother has written. She is to ask the Superior of the Sampierdarena house whether they still have the yellow cope.

A.M.F.

My Francesca,

1. Here I am writing to you again. I've just received Sr. A. Giacomina's letter and hear she wants to come on Tuesday. For charity's sake, she's not to come; when she is to come I'll write to her, as I told you. Imagine, she wants to go to Ovada! I won't have it, after [what] happened.1 Send for her and tell her I've written to you that when she is to go I'll write to her; for now let her stay; and then tell her whatever you think, but at once, so she won't leave.2

2. How are you? For charity's sake take care of yourself; try to keep well, for [...]3

3. Do me the kindness of asking the Superior whether they still have the yellow cope or have sent it to me, as (I) think. Tell me, do you remember anything about it? (I) think we had it here in Piacenza. Write and tell me something; ask Buon Pastore too, for I'd find it very useful.4

4. I hope soon to send you Sr. A. Serafina, so you can present her as vice-superior, your assistant. You'll see what a dear creature she is! I'm sending (le) the Biagini to Ovada.5

Goodbye; I want to be quick; your

[MADRE ROSA]

Sr.

1 Cf. L 274,3 and n. 4.

2 Cf. L 274,6.

3 She does not finish the sentence.

4 ask the Superior: Sr. A. Augusta Biagini. Ask Sr.

del Buon Pastore Dosi too. This Sister was at Sampierdarena for treatment.

5 Sr. A. Serafina, cf. L 273,1. To Ovada I'm sending the Biagini as Superior,

A. Carlotta, at present at Pennabilli.

The Superior has told her that he not only scolds but punishes and slaps the girls. Reminding him that it is for the Sisters to admonish the girls, she warns him she will not tolerate such behaviour any longer.

[Dear Sir],

1. If my health allowed, I would have come to see you in order to say better in person what I am about to tell you in writing.

2. Yesterday evening the Superior came and told me you had berated the girls.1 That would be nothing, but your having made a habit of punishing them, and adding the odd slap besides — you cannot imagine how painful this news was to me.2 Whereas you should bear in mind that correcting or admonishing them is our task.

3. I beg you, for charity's sake, to ensure it never happens again, otherwise I would be obliged to take other measures.3 I was sorry not to be able to see you on Sunday. If you would call today or tomorrow, we can come to a better understanding in person.

Sister ANNA ROSA GATTORNO

1 berated: ill-treated, harshly scolded.

2 This gentleman's arbitrary and violent behaviour wounded her deeply: you cannot imagine how painful this news was to me.

4 The protest is firm and forceful.

She is worried about the Sampierdarena house and the Superior's behaviour. She asks her to notify the Superiors about the Exercises to be held in Piacenza in July.

A.M.F.

My Francesca,

1. Yesterday evening I received your letter; I can't understand what you say, because I wrote to you the very day I went to Ferrara; true, I didn't write from Ferrara because I was in bed the whole time. Yesterday I sent you the paper for Sr. A. Elvira; today I'm sending you the petition, ready; it only needs to be sent or taken, as you think best.1

2. You can't believe how worried I am about the house; I hear there are horrifying things. Augusta is truly mad: she eats in her room, has the teacher wait on her, and so on and so forth. How dreadful, my God — a girl, and proud: that's the worst of faults!2

3. Tell the other Superiors they must all be here by 17 July for the holy Exercises; let them get ready.3

4. I'd like the exams to be held by the 15th, so the teacher could come too, and then whatever change is needed will be made.4 I don't think it wise for me to write to the Mayor for now; in person will be much better.

5. Keep watch over the Sisters, and I commend the portress to you; I've been anxious for several days; I'm afraid and don't know of what; the devil is cunning: where you think he's asleep, he's awake and stealing; please be careful. I'd like the portress to be an old woman.5

Goodbye, I'm in a hurry, your affectionate MADRE ROSA

Greet everyone for me.

What the Mother says in this paragraph is not clear, as the letter she is answering is missing. The paper for Sr. A. Elvira Persani, cf. L 282,1.

2 Anxious about the house: the Sampierdarena Institute, because of the rash conduct of the Superior Augusta Biagini, who isolates herself and has the teacher wait on her,

Sr. A. Tecla Mazzini.

3 The other Superiors: Sampierdarena, Sestri.

4 that change: transferring the Superior or the teacher.

5 She had held this view since the hospital opened. (Cf. L 199,4).

She urges her to send Sr. A. Giacomina to Piacenza with the postulant and to deliver the enclosed letter to Don Accinelli. She asks her to buy cloth and have a dress made for Carlotta.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Send me Sr. A. Giacomina at once. Call her to you at S. P. d'Arena, and when you have her safely there and she can't write to anyone, carefully, then send her with the postulant here to Piacenza; that will put an end to all correspondence and her eagerness to go to Ovada.1

2. Meanwhile I enclose this letter, which yesterday I forgot to put inside one to Don Accinelli; for charity's sake get it to him at once; see what it's about — he needs it immediately; while he's sending for the young Lady, they can take it to him.2

3. Yesterday Merli came, delighted with the flowers you sent him. If only they bore fruit, for I keep after him about the wall and the 500 F., but we never reach a [conclusion].3

4. I hope that by the end of next week you'll have Sr. A. Serafina with you; she'll act as vice-Superior and relieve you;4 I've received the basket, but I don't want you always sending me things, as you have too many expenses.

5. Listen, now I want something, but I absolutely don't want you to spend money: Carlottina needs an everyday dress of jaconet or calico; buy it from the Jews in my name, for I'll need other things later, and have it made at once, for the one she has is all old.4 They don't make them well here; I wanted to buy it here and send it to you, but they haven't any nice ones. You know the percale they have here is ugly. She keeps showing (mi) me the rags she has. Goodbye; for your guidance, tomorrow I leave for Ferrara and will stay 8 days; plan accordingly.6

Goodbye, your affectionate M. ROSA

1 Cf. L 276,1.

2 while he's sending for the young lady: no more precise information is available.

3 Merli, the municipal Secretary, long a friend and benefactor of the Institute.

The Mother wants him to plead her cause to obtain from the Municipality work on the boundary wall and a subsidy of 500 F.

4 Cf. L 276,4.

5 I don't want you to spend: she is to buy on credit from the Jews in her name cloth for an everyday dress (jaconet: a light cotton fabric, or calico: a very fine cloth).

6 plan accordingly as regards letters.

She protests at the failures to act and, as their mother, supports the Sisters' complaints.

[Dear Sir],

1. Hearing that you will not carry out the work I so justly asked for, I can no longer delay heeding my poor religious. I am their Mother and must act as such.1

2. I assure you it grieves me to the soul, for the good that might have come of it.2

Believe me, with all esteem and respect,

Sister ANNA ROSA GATTORNO

1 She firmly supports the Sisters' request.

2 The request is followed by the veiled but firm threat to withdraw the Sisters from the work. Cf. L 318, n. 5.

She has been to His Excellency the Bishop and spoke at length with Mgr Mariano. Carlotta must write to him at once. She begs Vincenza to take care of herself: the thought of her being ill makes her suffer, while if she is well she is consoled. She will let her know when she returns.

My daughter,

1. A line together with Carlottina,1 back from His Excellency's, where I spoke at length with Mgr Mariano; for charity's sake, my Vincenza, have Carlotta write a long letter to Mgr Mariano at once; I'll tell you why in person. So have her write at once, at once, and tell him lots of things, even about her conscience, and thank him for what he did for her in Rome, and say that if she hasn't written it was because she was waiting for the grace of hearing. In short, you know well what I mean.2

2. My dear Sr. A. Vincenza, the time has come when the good God is making me pay for all the sufferings you've endured because of me; I pay willingly and hope to suffer enough.3 Listen, my dear: if I nag you to look after yourself, believe me it's my own distress that drives me to torment you, because the mere thought that you might really fall ill makes me faint; so true is it that the illness I felt came precisely from the inner anguish I was experiencing.4

3. And I feel just as much consolation when I see you well; so if you want to do me the greatest kindness in this world, you must try to take care of yourself and keep healthy.

4. I'd gladly come on Saturday, but with all I still have to do it won't be until Monday evening; but I'll telegraph you. Troubles on every side, troubles! Plan accordingly about letters: none should arrive here on Monday.5 Please see that Carlotta writes at once, at once.

Goodbye, yours for all ages, amen.

M. ROSA

Dear Carlotta, write to Monsignor at once, for charity's sake; then I'll tell you everything in person and you'll laugh; your

affectionate M. ROSA

1 A line to Vincenza and Carlottina.

2 Mgr Mariano Wanstienkist had been very close to Carlotta in Rome.

He had surely regretted her failure to write, which the Mother tried to excuse.

3 She suffers at the thought that her dear Vincenza has suffered from the long, responsible and hard work she demanded of her, first in Piacenza and then at Ovada.

4 Now, at the mere thought that she might fall seriously ill, she feels faint.

5 She is to plan the correspondence so it arrives before Monday, the day she leaves Ferrara.

She sends the document for the power of attorney Sr. A. Elvira is to make. She wants Francesca to visit the Sampierdarena house to see how community life is going.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I arrived only yesterday evening at 7, and I'm writing today so you'll see I'm in Piacenza. I'm sending you this paper so that Sr. A. Elvira can make out the power of attorney to Mrs Liberati; if you lack the full names, you can write to this Lady, who will send them. I know her name is Carolina Liberati, No. 84 Via di Pietra, 3rd floor.1 Please be quick, for it's feared the deadline for these papers has already passed. For charity's sake, at once.

2. Meanwhile I'd like you to go to the house,2 for I hear there's unbelievable disorder. The Superior goes neither to prayers nor to the refectory; away with her, away, for pity's sake. I haven't time; I'll write more another time. Your affectionate M. ROSA

1 Sr. A. Elvira Persiani, from Rome, was to add the missing details for her power of attorney after asking Mrs Liberati in Rome for them.

2 That is, to the Sampierdarena Institute. Cf. L 278,2. Away, away: she means she must be moved to another house.

On the 29th anniversary of his pontificate she offers good wishes and asks blessings for the Institute.

Most Holy Father,

1. While the whole Catholic world, even from the remotest shores of the earth, is moved and rejoices with holy filial affection as the 16th of this month approaches — for on that day Your Holiness, by an example unique in the history of 19 centuries, begins the 29th year of your Pontificate — allow, Most Holy Father, the undersigned Superior of the Daughters of Saint Anne, in the name also of her whole Institute, to prostrate herself in spirit at your feet to express the filial sentiments of her heart.1

2. First, Most Holy Father, on that solemn day we shall all unite in prayer to thank the Lord for the long life granted to Your Holiness, surely not without great designs of Providence, and together we shall pray him to grant you a long series of years still, that you may see with your own eyes the triumph of Holy Church and the conversion of her enemies, sing the hymn of thanksgiving, and continue to govern Holy Church and your people in the ways of holiness and justice.

3. On this happy occasion I renew my warmest and most sincere thanks for all the spiritual and temporal favours Your Holiness has bestowed on the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne,2 favours which are a pledge of still greater ones which, I firmly trust, will lead us in future, so that, ever more united to the Apostolic See, we may share more abundantly in heavenly Blessings.

4. Finally I humbly beg you, Most Holy Father, to

bless the undersigned and with her all the Houses of the Institute, all the Sisters who compose it, the many schools they run, the hospitals and sick they care for and all their other works, so that, strengthened by the Blessing of the Vicar of Jesus Christ, they may advance ever further on the way of perfection until, their mortal course completed, they receive the Blessing of Jesus Christ our Lord.

Your Holiness's

Most humble and devoted daughter

Sister ANNA ROSA GATTORNO, Superior General of the Daughters of Saint Anne

1 The filial sentiments of her heart: sentiments of love and devotion rooted in her heart by his many expressions of goodwill and protection towards her and the Institute in its birth and spread, especially in Rome (where 4 houses had been founded in 1873).

2 All the favours: she does not name them, but has them clearly in mind and keeps their memory alive among her Daughters at every opportunity.

She asks for a 50% refund on some railway tickets already issued and for the reduction on the Roman Railways to be granted for the Sisters' charitable journeys.

1. The undersigned, Sister Anna M. Rosa Gattorno, foundress of the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne, who nurse the sick at home and in hospitals, informs Your Lordship that she applied to the Delegation Office of this Roman Railway for a 50% refund for some Sister nurses leaving Rome, and it was not granted, as this Office had no authorization from Your Honourable Lordship, although the letter of the Ministry of Public Works No. 3550/4729 of 6 September 1871, addressed to the Prefecture of Piacenza, was shown.

Hoping to obtain from Your Most Illustrious Lordship what she asks, the petitioner has the honour, with all esteem and respect, to sign herself Your Lordship's

Most humble Sister ANNA M. R. G.

She blesses the Lord for the good news of one Sister's nursing skills and advises having the others trained too. She gives instructions for the Superiors coming to Piacenza for the Exercises.

A.M.F.

My Francesca,

1. I've received your letter and note what you say about the Sister who pulls teeth and performs other operations. Blessed be God! Try to have others trained. You can't imagine how beneficial what the Sisters are doing will be for the work; word will spread and everyone will drop the bad opinion that the Daughters [of Saint Anne] were good for nothing.1

2. For the rest, do as you think best; we'll understand each other better in person. You can come on the 18th; the others should come on the 17th, as they begin that day.2 You can leave whichever [Sister] you think fit in charge for those 8 days.

3. Tell Sr. Augusta I'll tell her everything in person, as I haven't time.3 I assure you I'm so busy I don't know which way to turn. Carlotta is waiting for the dress and sends greetings; she's here and thanks you.4

In haste, your affectionate M. R.

4. Sr. A. Augusta will come with the teacher and together with the others; she'll leave as Superior whoever you think best, provided it isn't

Sr. A. Buon Pastore.5

1 The Sister who pulls teeth is Sr. A. Candida Carboneschi. "The Director has bought instruments specially for Sr. A. Candida to pull teeth and is very pleased with the Sisters." (Letter of Camisa to M. Rosa 27.6.'74).

2 The Superiors of the communities were to come to the Mother House for the Spiritual Exercises. Cf. L 278,3.

3 To the Superior of the Sampierdarena Institute. Cf. L 278,2; 282,2.

4 Cf. L 279,5.

5 with the teacher: Sr. A. Tecla Mazzini. Sr. A. del Buon Pastore was ill.

She explains the activities of the Daughters of Saint Anne and offers to send religious to nurse the sick, as he wishes.

Very Reverend Sir,

1. I learned this morning from the Rev. Sister of Charity at the Military Hospital that Your Reverence wishes to know the work of the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne and at the same time would like three of these Religious to nurse the sick in your town.1

2. I hasten to oblige. Our main work is nursing the sick in Hospitals and at home, of both sexes and every condition, accepting nothing in the sick person's house — neither pay, nor food, nor drink.

3. The Daughters of Saint Anne go through the streets and to the sick always two by two and nurse them night and day, never leaving the patient if he so wishes; in that case the nurses are relieved by another two, so the patient is never left alone.

4. We run schools for poor girls at risk up to 4th class, teaching them every kind of handiwork. We also teach poor little boys from 7 to 12, taking them all on Sundays to Mass, Confession and Communion. We teach catechism in the parishes.

5. As for sending you the Religious, I am entirely ready. The payment required is very small: fr. 400 a year and the house furnished with necessities — a little linen, furniture, etc.

6. I enclose my address: Stradone Farnese, Casa Figlie di S. Anna, Piacenza. With the greatest esteem and respect I remain Your Reverence's

Most humble Servant Sister ANNA ROSA GATTORNO

1 in your town: Polverigi, in the province of Ancona.

[Le]tter 287

Sr. A. FRANCESCA CAMISA

[Pi]acenza, 7 July 1874

She gives instructions for the departure of the Sisters and a postulant. She will send the teacher Onorata Colli to Sestri to prepare the girls for the exams. Francesca is to see about finding a confessor for the girls.

[A].M.F.

[My d]aughter,

1. I have an abyss of troubles on my back bowing me down; listen, I hear of the loud complaints at Sestri about that old woman from Ferrara, since she brought none of what she promised, and besides I was deceived, for she said she was good at teaching, and it's quite the opposite; so it's time we took a stand and relieved the Work of certain people who only harm it. What do you think? I'd like you to send her to me at once.1 If you agree, I'd like the girl to be the one who's in class with the teacher, for I'd like her to get her diploma, as Onorata is teaching there every day; so if you send her at once together with the old woman, that would be very good.2

2. Sr. A. del Salvatore will stay at Sestri for 8 days; for the exams of the S. P. d'Arena girls I'll see about taking Onorata, who in 20 days will get them to do what others can't do in a year.3 Try to send me the one I mention soon. I'm also inclined to leave the teacher, for from what she writes I see she's really not fit to be Superior. As the retreat is now only for Superiors, she can come with the others.4

3. Carlottina is waiting for the dress and fears it's been lost. For charity's sake, tell her something.5

4. Please see that others learn like Sr. A. Candida, as there's need.6

5. Tell me who hears the confessions of the religious of the house, and who says Mass. You say Don Antola is all ours; then why doesn't he hear the girls' confessions? Try to persuade him to do this work of charity.7

Goodbye, your Affectionate M. R.

1 The old woman from Ferrara: Rosa Borgonzoni, a widow of 65, who had pressed the Superior Sr. A. Paola Bucciotti so hard and had been accepted on references that later proved false. She had received the habit on 5.5.1874

and been sent to Sestri, where however she caused difficulties. She was dismissed from the Institute on 12 July 1874.

2 I'd like the girl (a postulant) in class with the teacher to get her diploma. Send her with the old woman so that Onorata Colli can prepare her.

3 At Sestri, replacing the Superior who is going to Piacenza for the Spiritual Exercises, Sr. A. del Salvatore Orsi will stay. To prepare the girls properly for the exams, she will send Onorata Colli to Sampierdarena.

4 This is the postulant; but not the teacher, Sr. A. Enrichetta Salvatelli, since the latter is not capable of acting as Superior.

She can come later with the other Sisters.

5 Cf. L 279,5.

6 Sr. A. Francesca replies on 9.7: "Sr. A. Innocenza" Dimari "is beginning to pull teeth".

7 The community has no confessor; Sr. A. Francesca went to the Archbishop, but he told her to find one herself. Don Antola said Mass every day in the hospital chapel.

A few words, as the Sisters are leaving. She commends them to her to be trained in nursing, as another Hospital is to be opened. She will soon leave for Invorio and will stop in Genoa on the way back.

My daughter,

1. Just a line, as the Sisters are leaving; I'd like you to train them for me, because I need them to open another Hospital.2 Ask the Director where he bought the dental instruments.3

2. How are you? I'm anxious; I hope you've received my unstamped letter. Listen, on Monday I leave for Invorio4 and then on the 19th I'll be in Genoa, which means you'll come back with me.

Goodbye, your affectionate [M. ROSA]. I've written everything to the Director.5

1 The date is taken from the context.

2 train them for me: give them practical nursing training.

3 A dental surgery had been set up in the Sampierdarena hospital.

4 Monday 13th, I leave for Invorio (Alessandria). Cf. App. IV.

5 Regarding the sending of the Sisters mentioned above.

She insists that other Sisters be trained along with Sr. A. Candida. Advice on the Sisters and the running of the Sampierdarena House while the Superior is away. Francesca is to find out whether Mgr Negrotto has arrived and invite him to her community, as the other Superiors should. She suggests she come to Piacenza for the feast of Saint Anne.

A.M.F.

My dear daughter,

1. I've just finished reading your letter, which the young nun delivered; though I'm breathless I want to reply. They had a good journey; your letter consoles me, but I'd like you to tell me there are others learning along with Sr. A. Candida. Ah, if only we could have at least three I'd be really happy; for you see, if she were lost to us, everything would be lost; try to do it; you'll see you'll be glad.1

2. Listen, I want the teacher left in the school and not made Superior on any account, for I realized she [is] not someone fit to be Superior; leave anyone else, but not her or Buon Pastore — I won't have it.2

3. Now the confessor: I'd be glad if you could arrange for him to keep away from the house; so let those Sisters who can come to confession at the Hospital, and the others rather to Don Accinelli, and then, little by little, he'll drop away.3

4. Mgr Negrotto must have arrived, for he left Rome on the 8th. Find out, and then it would be good for all the Superiors to go and each invite him to her house.4

5. Thank you for what you sent me, but it's too much; you mustn't. Enough, the Lord will repay you.

6. As for Sr. A. Elvira, send her to Genoa and I'll send you one from here. Do you know who'd be good for you? Sr. A. Raffaela: she's excellent in the kitchen, does very well and is so dear. See what you think; make whatever changes you see are needed;5 please keep an eye on the house while the Superior is here.6

7. If on the eve of Saint Anne's you can be sure the Archbishop isn't coming, you could leave after lunch by the last train and telegraph me, and I'll send someone to meet you at the station; then you'd enjoy the celebration; see what you can do; I'd love it; and you'd leave on Monday morning at 4 a.m. It's going to be a splendid celebration,7 and I assure you it wouldn't be complete for me without you; make sure and then come. Goodbye, your affectionate and for ever yours

MADRE R.

8. P.S. I hear you have some nuns being treated; see whether you could get the doctor to take Sr. A. Caterina; what good that would do our house! see what you can do, ask him; and Buon Pastore too; or at least Caterina.8 I'll pray a novena at once. It would be a blessing; for now knock and he'll open to you.

1 the young nun. It is not known who she was, perhaps one of the seven postulants who had received the habit on 17 April at the Sampierdarena Institute. Along with Sr.

A. Candida: she very much wants other Sisters, at least three, to learn from her how to pull teeth. They must make the most of it, for if she were lost a unique opportunity would be lost. Cf. L 287,4.

2 The teacher Tecla Mazzini. She is to give the task of temporarily replacing the

Superior (away for the Exercises) to anyone else, but not to the teacher nor to Sr. A. del Buon Pastore Dosi. Cf. L 285, n. 5.

3 The community's confessor was the "Parish Priest of Promontorio". Sr. A. Francesca had told her of some interference of his in the house (cf. letter of 19.3.74). The Mother suggests how the Sisters should act to make him withdraw.

4 Mgr Augusto Negrotto, cf. L 71, n. 3.

5 The changes needed for the smooth running of her hospital community.

6 the house: i.e. the Institute.

7 A splendid celebration: solemn and much talked about.

8 Some "Pietrine" Sisters were patients there. She suggests asking the doctor to take on Sr. A. Caterina and Sr. A. del Buon Pastore, both of the Sampierdarena Institute — at least Sr. A. Caterina.

She asks that the young candidates for the teaching diploma be examined by the Government Commission at the Institute.

Your Excellency,

1.
