The undersigned, Superior of the Daughters of Saint Anne, devoted to the moral and physical education of poor abandoned youth,1 having in her Institute several young women qualified to sit the examination for the diploma, who completed their teaching practice two years ago and obtained the School Inspector's certificate,2 begs Your Excellency to grant the favour that they need not take the examination in the public hall, but that the Honourable Examining Commission may come here to the House to examine them.3

2. Trusting to obtain this great favour from your kindness, so often experienced, she offers her most heartfelt thanks and humble respects, remaining with the greatest esteem Your Excellency's

Sister ANNA ROSA GATTORNO

1 abandoned youth: forsaken, neglected by their families.

2 Several young women: their number and names are unknown. Onorata

Colli had prepared them (cf. L 286,1), and they had done their practice and obtained the relevant certificate.

3 The Commission: the examining board.

She introduces the new Superior.

A.M.F.

My daughters,

1. The one who reads you this letter of mine is your Superior; prostrate yourselves on the ground and, kissing her humbly, promise her obedience, love and perfect submission.1

The Lord bless you. I am your affectionate MADRE ROSA G.

1 The new Superior: Sr. A. Carlotta Biagini, transferred from Pennabilli; they were to receive her in a spirit of faith.

She advises her on community and household matters and comforts her with her support.

A.M.F.

1. I'm answering yours, received the day before yesterday.1 Listen: first, I advise you always to send Sr. A. Rosa out, and I want you to put the one I've just sent you in the kitchen and have Sr. A. Rosa teach her;2 and send me Sr. A. Daria with the postulant. The postulant's uncle is paying her fare.3

2. Today you should receive fr. 300 from Count Galinelli, who supplies them on behalf of Countess Trotti;4 see that you get a written guarantee for the postulant's money: they're to give you fr. 30 every month.5

3. How taken aback I was by the accounts! My dear daughter, little by little you'll pay them. I called her and she assures me the chemist is owed only F. 100; she gave him the sixty, 60, and nothing is owed for this year 1874, because she always paid him. Just look, it's dreadful!6

4. God wills it so for my sins; soon I'll take the teacher away from you too and send you a very good one; write to your mamma, for charity's sake.7 Goodbye, your affectionate M.

Courage, and everything for Jesus. Listen: we'll appoint the assistants when I come, and the vice-superior too.8 Goodbye, your M...

1 The letter is of 25 July 74.

2 She had asked whether she should go shopping herself or ask the kitchen Sister, Sr. A. Rosa.

3 The postulant: Olga Fioraghi; cf. Reg. Post. n. 236.

4 Count Galinelli, Countess Maria Anna Trotti's new bursar

(replacing Giuseppe Squarzoni).

5 The postulant Fioraghi mentioned above.

6 The accounts. The new Superior wrote that she had found debts with some suppliers and with the chemist, including debts from 1872 and '73. The Mother enquired of the Superior Paola Bucciotti and tells her what remains to be paid to the chemist.

7 Her mother, Signora Giovanna Biagini, whom the Mother had met in Foligno.

8 About the Superior's assistants and the Vice-Superior. She wanted to know this too.

Willing to accept his request, she sets out the minimum conditions for sending the Daughters of Saint Anne.

1. I'm glad to answer your esteemed letter, the first I've had the pleasure of receiving, for which I thank you infinitely, hoping we may soon come and offer our poor services there too.1 You indicate that the means available to maintain the religious are few, so that at first there should be only three. I reply that since we cannot be fewer than four, the fourth will be at our expense.

2. Secondly, as for the house, it would be better if it had an entrance for the religious alone, but if that's not possible it doesn't matter, as long as the rooms are reserved solely for the religious, such as dormitories with iron beds, each with white curtains.2

3. There's no need to trouble about furniture; a table, a few chairs and a wardrobe for the linen will be enough. A few utensils will do for the kitchen.3

4. You also ask about the linen; provided it is new, it can be of any kind. The teacher will be qualified. The Institute is approved, and we are under the jurisdiction of the Bishops. Please accept, Reverend Parish Priest, my respectful greetings, while I remain with the greatest esteem and respect

Your Reverence's

Most humble Servant Sister ANNA ROSA GATTORNO

1 At Polverigi. Cf. L 286.

2 provided the rooms alone: at least the rooms should be kept for the Sisters only, for a minimum of privacy.

3 The bare minimum, with the utmost poverty and simplicity.

JJU

She asks for various news of the communities and people. She urges her to look after her health and to visit the Superior Augusta now and then.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I couldn't write sooner, being too busy; you sly thing, why didn't you come even on the day of the celebration?1 I understood everything.

2. I heard from your letter that you took Sr. A. Elvira to Genoa; you did well; whom did you take instead? As long as she's useful to you, all's well. Keep an eye on the Sestri Sisters;2 they'll have brought you the money; try to advise them to economize.

3. Did you go to Mgr Negrotto? How did he receive you? Did Don Accinelli go? Alessandro too, a visit of a few minutes. You'll have Fr Agostino with you; how is he?3 Have you put another Sister on teeth so she can learn? Write and tell me, because I didn't quite understand.4

4. I hope you've received the Rules and the other booklets.5

5. Try to take care of yourself; don't overdo it, for charity's sake; get help. What are those at the house doing? I can imagine, with that girl Sr. A. Augusta. If you can, try to visit her now and then.6 I'm stopping because I have no more time, otherwise I won't even get this off to you today.

Goodbye, my dear daughter; believe in the affection borne you by this ever your

Affectionate M. R.

1 She had invited her to the feast of Saint Anne. Cf. L 289,7. Nemo: not even.

2 Sr. A. Elvira Persiani was unhappy in the hospital and was not behaving well. Those at Sestri: the Sisters.

3 Mgr Negrotto (cf. L 71, n. 3) had gone to Genoa; Fr Agostino had gone there too, after a stay in Piacenza (cf. L 265, n. 5).

4 Another Sister to learn to extract teeth (cf. L 289,1).

5 the Rules. A text of the Constitutions had been printed with the ad experimentum approval of 12 June 1874 by the Cardinal Protector Luigi Vannicelli.

The author was certainly Fr Tornatore.

6 Those at the house: the Institute. That girl Sr. A. Augusta (cf. L

278,2; 282,2; 285,3) caused her great worry by the way she behaved.

She suggests how to explain to a postulant the conditions for her acceptance and how to treat a Sister. She also announces a Sister's transfer and the arrival of two others.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I've received your letter and note what you say about the postulant. See whether at least she's healthy, for I fear she isn't, and you can tell her that if within a year she isn't well I intend to send her home; and make sure at least the 15 F. a month you mention are guaranteed, and let her write to her uncles to reassure them. In short, let her do what she must, and send her at once.1

2. In a few days Sr. A. Cecilia will reach you; for charity's sake keep a firm hand on her; don't let her stay in church except during recreation, and if she says anything, let her know it's my order. If she thinks she can do nothing, send her to the sick; give her the wardrobe keys.2 You can send me Sr. A. Rosa; that will be good; I'll send you another two, good and obedient.

3. I'm glad to hear you're trying to clear the debts; well done. Courage. Listen: that person who came to see you — I warn you not to trust him; I can say no more for fear this letter goes astray.3 Listen, write to that postulant not to worry; we'll send her trunk tomorrow with the receipt, and I'll soon send her watch; let her be patient, for I forgot.4 Ask Sr. A. Rosa whether they gave her the things she had there; if not, give them to her.

Goodbye, in haste; I am your affectionate

M. R.

As for the girls, do as you think best.

1 As the letter M. Rosa is answering is missing, no further details of the postulant are known. The Mother advises her how to reply and on what conditions she could be accepted.

2 Sr. A. Cecilia Tortini; keep a firm hand on her = be firm in demanding what

I tell you, and if she refuses, tell her it's my will. If she thinks she can stay idle, make her work.

3 that person: she does not name him, fearing the letter might fall into other hands; she repeats it some time later, cf. L 319,4 and the relevant note.

4 write to that postulant: nothing further is known about this.

She gives precise, detailed orders about the house door, comings and goings, and the portress's duties.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I want what I write carried out. These are my orders: the door that used to serve as the house door is to be shut tight, the key kept by you, locked in your drawer, and on no account is anyone to go out through that door again. There must be only one house door.1

2. I'll soon send you a portress, and she is never to be taken from her post for any reason. She'll have sufficient instructions to do her duty, which she'll hand to you in writing, so that if she fails you can reprove her and give her the prescribed penances.2

3. If the coal can't come in through the usual door, you may open this one that's to be kept shut, but no other; and when that happens the portress must be present too, for not even you may open this door without the Sisters seeing and knowing that it's opened for an unavoidable reason.3

4. The house door must be kept locked, so that when the nurses go out they can't leave unless the portress opens it. If the portress isn't there, you'd do well to ask Don Accinelli to have a bell fitted: one ring for the portress, three for the Superior, four for the cook.4 I want this done at once.

This postulant really is a goose, and old besides.5 Goodbye in haste, your affectionate M. R.

1 Something unpleasant had happened. Sr. A. Assunta Saccini had left the house without anyone knowing, determined to leave the Institute. "They found her in S. Lorenzo some hours later, brought her to my house, and she refused to go back to the nuns

... I decided to send her to Piacenza." So Don Antonio Accinelli to the Mother

(letter of 7.8.1874). The Mother decides on the measures to be taken immediately.

2 I'll soon send you a Sister with the permanent office of portress, who will be given the proper instructions.

3 If the coal cannot be brought in through the main (usual) door,

let the side door be opened with the portress present, for not even (nemo) you, the Superior, may open it without the Sisters seeing and knowing that it is opened for an incontrovertible reason.

4 If the Sister portress is momentarily absent when the Sisters need to go out, she can be called with one ring of the bell; with this signal the Superior can also be called (three rings) and the cook (four).

5 The Superior had sent the above Sister to Piacenza with a postulant: "a Genoese widow aged fifty", accepted by Don

Accinelli, as he himself writes on 3 July 1874.

Receiving no letters, she fears Francesca is ill. She invites her to come to Piacenza for at least a day and asks her to speak to Alessandro.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I've had no letters from you for more than 12 days. Are you ill? For charity's sake, if so have someone write to me, if [you can't do it yourself]. Listen, have you received two letters from me? Did you go to the Archbishop? What did he say?1

2. I'd like you to come over here at once for twenty-four hours; we can settle everything in person; I'll add nothing more; I'm expecting you, or a letter if you're ill, which I don't believe;

your affectionate M. R.

3. I've just received your letter. I note what you say about A... Patience; you'll hear everything in person; leave Sr. A. Candida as vice-Superior, so you'll feel safer, and for the door you can put Sr. A. del Buon Pastore provisionally. What do you think? If she does well you'll keep her; if not she'll be changed.2

4. Send for Alessandro and tell him that when you come here I'll think about taking him away from Genoa for a month for a change of air.3 On your return you'll tell him everything, but I don't want him to tell anyone what you say; then you'll hear more and tell him in person what I want. Tell him to be good and obey me, and I'll do a great deal for him. Goodbye, your affectionate

M. R.

1 Did you go to the Archbishop? She was to invite him to bless the hospital chapel reserved for the Sisters. Cf. L 207, n. 4.

2 what you say about A.: the Superior Augusta, and her difficulties in governing the Sampierdarena Community. She may leave Sr. A. Candida Carboneschi in charge during her short absence, and as portress

Sr. A. del Buon Pastore Dosi (then under treatment in the hospital, cf. L 289,8), who may stay on as part of the community if she does well.

3 Alessandro. He was staying with Don Accinelli, but his escapades had made relations difficult. (Cf. letters of Accinelli 3 and 7 August 1874).

She is glad of the news about Alessandro and sends 100 francs for him. It is not true that Don Accinelli is displeased with Francesca; on the contrary he praised her. She urges her to act shrewdly with the Superior of Sampierdarena.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I've received your letter1 and hear about Alessandro; I'm very glad; I'm sending you F. 100; give them to him and tell him to use them carefully.2

2. Accinelli isn't at all displeased with you; on the contrary he praised you to the skies, endlessly; he only took offence because you told the carpenter. Enough; for charity's sake try not to upset him; he's full of good intentions and says he's very fond of Alessandro, and if he tells him anything it's for his good; and we've agreed to build the Confessor's little flat, for whom I hope to find someone very soon.4 For the rest, please do things tactfully so he isn't upset, for charity's sake, because I'll tell you certain things in person that will surprise you.

3. Sr. A. A., you understand me, says one thing to you and another to him.5 I hear she has endless debts, and do you know what she does? Every moment she goes or sends the teacher to Genoa to fetch money, and do you know how much he's already given her? More than 1,000 F. How dreadful! And when he says anything: "Francesca ordered it so"! But I see she manages the money badly and can't make it go far. The religious, as you said, eat badly; there isn't a penny's worth of provisions in the house; everything is bought day by day; how dreadful!

4. Signora Airenta is upset because they didn't promptly return what she'd lent them, and then, when she sent for them, they gave them back broken. What do you think of that? And the most worthy Superior didn't deign to show herself to Maria, but had a girl hand them over. How dreadful! She has declared she'll never lend her anything again.6

5. Accinelli took these things very badly, and he's not wrong. What do you think? Enough, in person; certainly you don't know; they're making a fine mess of things.

6. Mgr N. too was not pleased with Augusta;7 but he couldn't stop talking about you and was very pleased. You see he noticed this as well. Enough, it will soon be remedied. Give Alessandro [the money].

Your affectionate MADRE ROSA

Goodbye; the Lord bless you, strengthen you with his grace and make you happy.

1 The letter she is answering is of 19 August.

2 Alessandro was examined by the hospital Director, who prescribed the Savignone baths and a course of treatment. He is waiting for the money. He goes about with his uncle Federico.

3 Don Accinelli had gone to Piacenza with Mgr Augusto Negrotto on 17

August (cf. letter to M. Rosa 15.8.74).

4 for the confessor, cf. L 243, n. 2.

5 The Superior Augusta is not sincere with her; the Mother had warned her of this.

6 Signora Paola Airenta, a friend of Mother Rosa and on good terms with the

Sisters of the Institute. What she lent is not specified. The most worthy Superior did not apologize or show herself to Maria (perhaps the maid).

She, Signora Airenta, decided to lend her nothing more.

7 Mgr Negrotto too was unfavourably impressed by Sr. A.

Augusta.

Two Sisters will arrive from Piacenza, and she gives instructions about them. She has asked Don Accinelli to send to Ovada the other two she mentioned.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I'm sending you two Sisters; one is Sr. A. Colomba, who is for the wardrobe, on condition that you never let her go out — never — neither to the sick nor for anything whatever. She's capable, also at writing, so on feast days she can teach everyone. Never let her open the door, never.1

2. Tell Don Accinelli that when he was here asking me for this ironer, (I) she hadn't come to mind. She makes shirts very well and you can take in such work, and she'll teach the Sisters, especially the young ones; it's good for them to learn. Please keep her busy so she isn't idle.2

3. Tell the steward at Castello that I'll be in Genoa by the end of September, that I send him warm greetings and always remember him in my wretched prayers.3

4. The other of these Sisters is Sr. A. Geronima, who is for the sick; but you must always send her with someone you can trust, for she has a tongue that wags very fast.4

5. I've asked Don Accinelli to send two of those you have to Ovada.5 He'll tell you their names. On Monday at 4 p.m. they'll be at the station;6 try to meet them and put them in the omnibus, so they'll be less seen. I forgot to give Don Accinelli the signed tickets for those leaving for Ovada.7 I'm sending them by Sr. A. Colomba. Goodbye, your affectionate M. ROSA

1 Sr. A. Colomba Chianale had received the religious habit on 30 September

1873. On condition. She was given very specific tasks in the house, so she was not to go out, either to nurse the sick, beg or run other errands, nor to be put at the door as a substitute.

2 the shirts: summer shirts with small pleats in front. You can take in such work, and it will bring in income. She can also teach the Sisters. Please find her work.

3 The steward: perhaps the manager of the House at S. Maria di Castello, previously occupied by the community.

4 The other is Sr. A. Geronima Piralli, for nursing. For her the usual advice: give her a trustworthy companion, for she's an incorrigible chatterbox (cf. L 216, n. 6).

5 of those you have: Sisters of the community.

6 The two new ones will be at the station: Sr. A. Colomba and Geronima.

7 the signed tickets: the vouchers for the rail reduction.

She copies for her a letter written to Canon Rinaldo De Giovanni about the arrangements for buying premises in Rome. She asks for news of her, of the Sisters and of the work, and wishes her a pleasant holiday.

Most Illustrious Marchioness,

1. I send you the copy I sent to the Rev. Canon Degiovanni, as we agreed before I left, he having already sent me the bonds.1

2. "I received the 16 bonds of fr. 60 and the 14 of fr. 25, and that is in order; the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne is ready to contribute to the purchase of the premises by paying Fr. 6,000, retaining bonds corresponding to that sum. These bonds are not to be drawn but immediately regarded as extinguished.2

3. The purchase of the House must however be so made that, while registered in the name of the Pious Union, it is declared at the same time that, the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne having paid fr. 6,000 towards it, should they be dismissed by the Direction of the Pious Institute, or for other reasons, the Superior General of the Daughters of Saint Anne shall have the right to occupy as her property a part of the house designated and described in the contract itself.3

4. When Your Reverence considers my proposal fair and the house to be bought is ready, I shall come to Rome or send someone to represent me for drawing up the contract, and the L. 6,000 will be paid immediately and the remaining bonds corresponding to the agreed sum withdrawn at the same time. Meanwhile kindly write to me about it so that I can make provision."

5. That, my dear Marchioness, is what I wrote to the Rev. Canon Degiovanni.4 As the occasion gives me the pleasure of writing to you, I come eagerly to ask for news of you, of which I have long been entirely deprived.5

6. I will not hide from you how this silence grieves me, for I fear I have displeased you in some way. Since I left I have never had a letter confirming your satisfaction with the Religious: whether they do their duty, whether their work is as you wish; in short, dear Marchioness, give me all this news that concerns us both.6

7. I prefer to think my letters have gone astray, or that your immense charitable and family occupations have prevented you.

8. Trusting that this time you will heed my request and send me two lines for my peace of mind, I wish you and all your family a pleasant holiday, asking you to present my respects to your most worthy Husband and warm greetings to your charming girls.

While I remain, Marchioness, yours,

Sister ANNA ROSA GATTORNO

1 In the following paragraphs (2-4) she copies the central part of the letter she sent to Canon Degiovanni.

2 She acknowledges the bonds and tells him how she intends to use them.

3 The purchase... itself. The house to be bought is to be registered to the "Pious

Union of Lady Protectors of Domestic Servants", but the deed of purchase must include the clause concerning the Daughters of Saint Anne, who contributed

F. 6,000 to the purchase.

4 The Marchioness replies on 28 August: "thank you, but I have nothing to do with it;

I leave it entirely to you and him, for I understand nothing about it".

5 She assures her she wrote to her and to Anna Carrega and regrets that

"it's not the first time the post has played such tricks".

6 "Your dear Sisters certainly cannot have displeased me, for on the contrary I have done all I could to have them placed at Frascati and hope to succeed." This is the reassuring reply. (AFSA, Friends).

She has received the little paper and asks for another copy. She speaks of one of the new Sisters and of visits she will soon make to two houses.

A.M.F.

My blessed daughter,

1. A line to tell you I've received the little paper; how I'd like a few more copies, but for charity's sake don't say I'm the one who wants them; what can I do, I had to promise Fr Agostino I'd write to you about it; for my part I wanted to burn this one too, but they say it will help make God's Work known, and when it's a question of that I'm ready to make any sacrifice.1

2. Now these two Sisters: take Sr. A. Colomba with you when you go to S. P. d'Arena, and to Albaro, so she gets some fresh air and doesn't fall ill;2 otherwise you'll see she'll work very well for you and you'll be pleased. She promised me to do well and teach the Sisters with charity and humility.

3. As for the two you're to send to Ovada, whom I mentioned to Don Accinelli, wait until I write to you again.3

4. And tell the steward I'll be with you in Genoa at the end of September.4 I leave on Monday and hope to get through things quickly.5 I'll be at Nizza 8 or 10 days and then at Ovada. If he wishes to write to me about anything urgent, let him write; I'll be very glad to receive his letters.

5. I'm also glad to hear of the observance. Greet all the Sisters for me and tell them I send them my blessing, wishing it upon them from Heaven, that the Lord may give them perseverance.

Goodbye, your Affectionate M.

1 The little paper: La Settimana Religiosa di Genova, 23 August 1874. In the column Memorie Storiche Genovesi it published a short article: Cenni sull'Istituto delle FSA, on their charitable activity, particularly in Genoa. She asks for some copies; she had promised Fr Agostino to ask for them.

2 As Sr. A. Colomba has demanding work in the house, she suggests taking her along when she goes out of Genoa so she gets a little fresh air. Cf. L 299,1-2.

3 For the two: cf. L 299, n. 5.

4 the steward: cf. L 299,3.

5 I leave on Monday, 31 August.

She is pleased with the news from Sestri but cannot say the same of Sampierdarena. She will send a Sister; Francesca may accept the girl and send her as soon as possible. She speaks of Carlotta's grief over a recent disappointment in love. She has had a consoling letter from Alessandro.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I've just received your letter and hear what you've done for Sestri; I'm very pleased and content;1 but I'm extremely upset about S. P. d'Arena, hearing how she treats the religious, her lack of thrift and her conduct. What she did at Signora Airenta's — which you surely don't know about — is truly detestable; horrible!2

2. You ask about going to see the prize-giving; go by all means; it will help you when they have to be given at the house, for I hear Accinelli wants to give them soon.3

3. You mention Sisters and I don't know what you mean; I don't understand. I'd be inclined to send you Sr. A. Battistina as portress, because I want to send Sr. A. Geltrude to Rome; are you happy with that?4 As for the girl, accept her with the 80 F. and send her as soon as you have the chance.5

4. Carlotta is utterly heartbroken; nothing will come of what she was hoping for, poor thing. I feel truly pierced, for it's clear she had set her heart on it, and now I've had to give her the verdict; you can imagine. Now I'm sending her to Genoa with Onorata to take her mind off it, and then she'll go to her aunt's and come to you. With this company I hope she'll enjoy herself and get over it. What a world! She'd be happy if they hadn't put these foolish ideas into her head, which only rob the heart of peace. Poor thing, she pours out her heart in church, but it's pitiful... You can imagine my sorrow; I can't express how great it is, if only from seeing her suffer.6

5. Tell me, did Alessandro leave you his address? Meanwhile I'm sending you this [letter] for him; forward it; I've received a letter from Alessandro that consoled me greatly; he assures me he's being good and sensible; what a consolation! It makes up for so many others.7

6. I hope to be with you without fail by the end of September; so I've decided to write to the Superior Augusta to submit to rendering accounts to Don Accinelli and handing him the whole temporal administration, for the deficit is now too great and we can't go on; she tells you one thing and does another. Enough, I'll come and we'll put everything right.8

7. So I approve everything you've done and are doing; courage. I have so many things to tell you, good and bad; you'll hear, but all for Jesus and in Jesus; I bless you a thousand times, while I remain your affectionate... MADRE ROSA

1 She had gone to Sestri, looked into how the work was going and given appropriate advice.

2 of Sampierdarena. As usual, the Superior does not change. Cf. L 298, 3 and 4.

3 She had been invited by the "Pietrine Sisters" to the prize-giving at the end of the school year in their state school. Give at the house:

at the Institute.

4 Sr. A. Battistina Bertuzzi; she wanted to transfer Sr. A. Geltrude Gottelli to

Rome.

5 During her visit to Sestri, a member of the administration had put forward a young postulant.

6 Carlotta is heartbroken at the bitter disappointment of her "first love". The Mother feels the pain keenly and takes it to heart with empathy.

7 Alessandro was at Savignone for the baths prescribed by the doctor (cf. L 298, n. 2).

8 Cf. L 298,3. A remedy is finally needed; she had been patient, trying every means in vain.

She describes in detail her journey and the welcome she received at Nizza. She greets Carlotta and all the Sisters, to whom she intends to write.

My daughter,

1. Here I am, having already dined and wholly intent on writing to you and telling you about my journey in detail. From Piacenza to Alessandria it was dreadful; I felt I was dying between the headache and everything else. On arriving at the station I took out the mint water and soaked my handkerchief with it; in the end, by dint of this water – which for me is a true balm – I revived and the atrocious headache that had seized me mercilessly went away. So, what to do? We had to stay in the station from one until three; I had a coffee, and that too did me good. How I would have liked to have a little of that food you give me when I make long journeys, but this one is very long, from 9 until 4[½]. What a horror, never again! Sr. A. Benedetta ate a good piece of roast beef with potatoes, and as for me, patience; the fear of a headache frightened me thoroughly. I had an egg brought, but what can you expect, it was one of those laid in the year 1871; well then, God accepted my sacrifice, the coffee restored me, and I made the rest of the journey suffering much less.1

2. When I arrived at the station there was a cloud of boys, and the good Count Galvagno, and the Superior, who had prepared a magnificent dinner for me. I found everything very well, everything in order.2

3. You will tell Carlottina — enough, I will write to her now; you will tell the religious that I am most grateful to them for all [that] they did to show the affection they bear me; mine is certainly no less, but of this I reserve the right to say a couple of words to them another day.3

4. Vincenza, my beloved daughter, be assured that I always carry you with me, and I repeat to you what I have told you a thousand other times: that no one will ever take your place, for all eternity, no, no; “My God, you see it and you can vouch for it!”.4

Your affectionate MOTHER. The Parish Priest is coming; otherwise it will not go to the post.5

1 Amid so many annoyances, troubles and sufferings, a humorous note: the egg of 1871!

2 The welcome is festive: a large group surrounding the person of note: Count Annibale Galvagno and the Superior Sr. A. Giuseppa Troni at the station, and at home, the magnificent dinner.

3 you will tell Carlottina. She does not continue because she has decided to write to her; you will tell the religious: she expresses her gratitude for the demonstrations of affection on the occasion of her name day on 30 August. The feast of St Rose of Lima was then celebrated on 30 August.

4 She is now also helped by Sr. A. Benedetta Carrega. It is right to reassure Sr. A.

Vincenza: no one will take her place; it is hers by right always, in time and in eternity.

5 The Parish Priest, Fr Ludovico Bisio, is coming; she hands him the letter, otherwise the dispatch would have to be delayed.

She asks her to send some personal belongings she forgot and to deliver to the Father the enclosed letter.

My daughter,

1. Here is another letter from me. Listen, do me the kindness of sending me at once my shawls, which I forgot;2 and I urge you to watch Sr. A. Irene very carefully, that she not be with you-know-who, do you understand?3 You cannot believe how lost I feel being alone, without you or Carlotta.

2. Put among the shawls a silk cap of mine that I keep in the drawer of the chest, the washed one that still needs ironing, for I need it at night, since I cannot wear the kerchief, which suffocates me.

3. Goodbye, for I want to write a couple of lines to Carlotta and also to that person to whom you will take care to give it, or have it delivered safely. Your affectionate M. R.

4. P.S. When you asked me whether Sr. A. Battistina should go to S. P. d'Arena alone and I answered yes, I forgot to tell you that she must go with Sr. A. Giacomina, and both must go to S. P. d'Arena, since the Superior there already [knows] what to do with them.4

1 Given its content and the correlation of the dates and events of the correspondence, this letter should be dated September, not August.

2 On leaving, she had forgotten some personal belongings.

3 Sr. A. Irene Carmeli. She was not to stop and chat with Sr. A. Eletta Bruschi. (Cf. L Rapallino to M. Rosa, 9.9.74).

4 Sr. A. Battistina Bertuzzi and Sr. A. Giacomina Schenardi were to go to the Superior Francesca Camisa, already informed of their arrival.

Two Sisters will arrive: one for her community, whom she will try to train for the hospital, the other whom she must accompany to Sestri. She is very displeased at the transfer of Sr. A. Giovannina, made without her knowledge. She will be in Genoa after finishing her visit to Nizza and Ovada.

My daughter,

1. I am at Nizza; at Piacenza, where I received yours, I was unable to answer you to thank you for the lovely present you sent me for St Rose. How obliged I am to you, my daughter, and dearer to me than the present was the news you gave me of the hospital. May God be blessed for ever.

2. On Saturday at the latest you will have Sr. A. Battistina as portress; what can I say, I have a feeling that she will learn as Candida learned; what do you think? Is it so? How glad I would be! Enough; for charity's sake, do all you can, for I hope that with God's help you will succeed in everything. Sr. A. Giacomina will come too, and she will be for Sestri; you will go and install her, and for the moment you will send the other to Genoa, for I will write to the Superior about how she is to keep her. I want you to do everything without others having to meddle, do you understand me? You will give Sr. A. Giacomina whatever instructions you, being on the spot, think fit.1

3. You tell me they want one to go out begging, but how are so many religious to support themselves? They want, and the means are few; they must be made to understand this a little.2

4. I hear that they have now sent Sr. A. Giovannina there and that they did this without my order; if you see her, and indeed try to have her come to you, the most worthy Superior of Genoa, make her understand that I am displeased, because when I wrote to her that I do not want any changes or transfers of Sisters made without my order, and she instead takes the liberty of doing as she pleases, it means my orders are worth little. If she was ill, she should have written to me and I would have thought about moving her wherever I saw best.3

5. There they are killing my nurses and then would not want to say so.4 I am most displeased, because meanwhile I had assured people that she is in Genoa, and instead her relatives found her somewhere else, and this shows that things are not going well.5

6. Enough, I shall soon be in Genoa; meanwhile I shall go first of all to the hospital to embrace you (you) and spend at least a whole night and a day there. Write to me here, for I shall stay 10 or 12 days, but then I shall stay less at Ovada.

Goodbye; for charity's sake, take care of yourself, do not make me worry. Yours for all ages

M. R...

1 Sr. A. Battistina Bertuzzi will be portress at the hospital, cf. L 302,3. She has the feeling, foresees, that she will learn, like Sr. A. Candida, to extract teeth. Cf.

L 285,1. Sr. A. Giacomina Schenardi: she will accompany her to Sestri, as Superior;

you will go and present her, and you will temporarily send the other to Genoa. I will write to the Superior: cf. L 306,2.

2 In the House at Sampierdarena they want a religious solely for begging. They want more Sisters and have few means.

3 They sent Sr. A. Giovannina Pizzorno there without my order.

4 They are killing my nurses: they make them ill and take little care of them.

5 I am most displeased. To the relatives who at Nizza had asked her for news and the

Sister's address she had said that she was in Genoa, and instead they had then found her at Sampierdarena.

She tells her that the Superior of Sestri will come to her to recover, and gives instructions about this. She urges her not to overburden the Sisters with work and to provide them with good, substantial food.

My daughter,

1. I have been at Nizza since yesterday and have not been able to thank you for the lovely present you sent me on St Rose's day, because I had no time, and also I was a little displeased because it seemed to me that you had not carried out my orders.1 Enough. Now I write about something else and hope to be obeyed.

2. I will send, or rather, the Superior of Sestri will come there for some time, perhaps only a few days, and I want her not to go to the sick; let her stay there on the grounds of recovering. Meanwhile she may sew and help the wardrobe keeper, but let her not be treated differently; good.2

3. I hope everything was done not for lack of good will, but because so often one reflects too little; enough, be of good heart.3

4. I am very glad to hear that providence does not fail you, nor do the sick; I urge you not to overwork the religious too much. If you want others whom you need, I will send them to you, but for charity's sake let them not be worn out.4

5. A little pure wine if they need it; let dinner and supper be nourishing food. For charity's sake, let them not eat vegetables, because they weaken too much.

6. I would like you to buy a small box of pills from the Capuchins and send it to this address: To the Superior

Sr. A. Domenica, Piazza S. Agata No. 1, Casa Figlie di S. Anna, Rome;5 and likewise another to Sr. A. Vincenza, for both of them are in extreme need of them.

Greet all the Sisters for me, and believe me yours

Affectionately, M. ROSA

1 Transfers of Sisters had been arranged without informing her. Cf. L 305,4,5.

2 The Superior of Sestri: Sr. A. Filomena Pugnaloni. Let her keep to what has been arranged.

3 I hope everything: refers to what she mentioned above, in Para. 1.

4 not to overwork: not to subject them to heavy strain and excessive fatigue.

5 To the Superior Domenica Marchesini.

She thanks her for the present sent for her name day and urges her to send the list of debts left by the previous Superior. She longs to hear that all the debts are paid. Write to her at Nizza, or else at Genoa.

My daughter,

1. Thank you for the lovely present you sent me; I am very grateful to you for it, but I fear you have all deprived yourselves of what you need, knowing you to be so hard pressed. For charity's sake, see that nothing is lacking.

2. I hope you have received the month's money;1 I want you to send me the whole list of the accounts the other Superior left you, for I wish to have them. I cannot wait for you to write to me: “Mother, the accounts are settled and we have a little in store”.2 And besides, I already know your skill at economizing, so I shall see everything carried out as I wish.

3. I am at Nizza, as you see from the date; if you have to write to me you can address it here; I shall stay 10 or 12 days and then go to Ovada, but I shall stay only a few days in that house, so you can address your letters to Genoa, where I shall be at the end of the month, or else here.3

Goodbye; greet the Sisters for me, and receive many embraces in the heart of Jesus, where I leave you, as I sign myself your

Affectionate M. Has Sr. A. Cecilia arrived? See that she works.4

1 The subsidy from Countess Maria Anna Trotti and the fees of the resident girls.

2 the whole list; the Superior sends her the accounts on 7 September. A debt of 100 francs remains.

3 Cf. L 305,6.

4 For Sr. A. Cecilia cf. L 295,2. The Sister arrived on 9 September.

[The] number of patients treated in the hospital has kept growing during the Sisters' eight months of service. She therefore asks that the sum originally agreed be increased.

Honourable Congregation of Charity,

1. The undersigned turns with a request to Your Most Illustrious Lordships, that what she asks may be granted. The scarcity of provisions, and the very great number of patients who entered and occupied this Civil Hospital during these eight months, amounting to 64, mean that not infrequently I have had to send it help so as to be able to continue.1

2. The goodness and charity of Your Most Illustrious Lordships assure me that you will take my request into consideration and increase the agreed sum.2

Confident of obtaining everything, with the highest esteem I remain Your Most Illustrious Lordships'

Sister ANNA ROSA GATTORNO

1 The Congregation of Charity, in the Agreement drawn up at the opening of the hospital, 12 January 1871, undertook to pay the Daughters of Saint Anne L.

3,000 a year for the upkeep of 10 patients.

2 With humble firmness she asks for recognition of the rights of the patients and of the

Sisters.

She writes at one in the morning, unable to stay in bed because of acute suffering. She asks her to pray, as she is in great anguish over what Fr Ricchini means to do and over what is happening in two communities in Rome. Sr. A. Palmira is to leave for Rome at once, and Vincenza is to tell her how to behave with the M. President and about the house.

Dear daughter,

1. I have been writing since one o'clock after midnight; I got up because I could not bear to stay lying down for the tremendous pain I feel; I went to bed at 11 and had to get up, because I am suffering too much.1

2. Listen, let the Fr tell you everything, because having so many things to tell you I have no time to relate what Fr Ricchini means to do, and I greatly fear they have compromised Alessandro for me.2 Have prayers said, there is nothing else; then I received dreadful letters from Rome about the muddles they are making at Tor de' Specchi; for charity's sake send Sr. A. Palmira at once, for today I am writing to them to obey her as their Superior.3

3. They need a cook; you could send to Cortemaggiore again to fetch Sr. A. Daria, or else clothe someone, but I would think it better not to; instead, first give Sr. A. Daria a good dressing-down, that is, instruction; if that person is not there, do it (by) yourself.4

4. Listen, they write to me that they have no mattresses on the beds and that the dirt is such that they do not know where to sleep, and that the Superior of Trastevere has sent them two girls to sleep there without sending their sheets or their beds, and that they have ailments; in short, it is a horror, they do not even cook, and sad rumours are already going about.5

5. For charity's sake, do at once what I am writing to you; I hope you can get money for the journey; and at the Morte you will put Sr. A. Eufemia; if two religious arrive from Foligno, Sr. A. Pierina is to be kept at the Morte, that is firmly decided, because she is consumptive; the other, Sr. A. Graziosa, you will have examined, and if you hear she has nothing wrong you will put her in the House.6 If that countryman, Sr. A. Sabina's father, had two rooms so that the sick little girls could be taken there for a while, together with two nuns, see what that Person says to you.7

6. Meanwhile you will tell Sr. A. Palmira how she is to conduct herself with the M. President, and likewise about cleanliness, about everything. If you could give her some 30 or 40 F., if you have them;8 be sure to inform her well, and if Mgr Negrotto has the Parrocchietta closed, let them close too, telling the M. President that it is he who wants it, which means it will be the Pope's wish.9

7. At once, for charity's sake, and meanwhile I am writing to them. There, it is almost three. Oh, how long this night is! If I have forgotten anything, see that you do it. For charity's sake, let Sr. A. Eufemia come for lessons and study.

Goodbye, dear Vincenza; if you were here I would come and call you, and then my agitation would pass. Goodbye; greet Carlotta for me and believe me, on earth as in heaven, your affectionate M.

I have received the shawls, thank you.10 Give this letter to the usual Person.11

1 She is very ill. Cf. L 312,1.

2 Fr Tornatore will tell you Ricchini's intentions and actions. Fr Accinelli had informed the Mother in these terms: “Fr Paolo Ricchini (brother of Fr Angelo), wishing to reply to the ‘Settimana Religiosa’, which had given a note on the foundation of the Daughters of Saint Anne (cf. L 301,1), wrote a long article from which it emerged that his brother had done everything on the advice” of Archbishop Magnasco and of his Vicar in bringing the lawsuit. Cf. L 84, n. 2. I greatly fear. Alessandro would have liked to intervene in his mother's defence, but had been dissuaded. (Cf.

L Accinelli to M. Rosa, 6 September 74).

3 The Superior, Sr. A. Eletta Bruschi, had left Tor de' Specchi. Let Sr. A. Palmira go at once to replace her.

4 A cook is needed there; let Sr. A. Daria go, after being well instructed in what she must do and how she must behave.

5 This, in brief, is the situation she referred to in para. 2.

6 Instructions concerning some Sisters. For Sr. A. Pierina Tea she has made the decision to send her to the infirmary because she is ill with consumption; Sr. A. Graziosa

Danieli is to go to the Mother House, if no serious illness is found.

7 Sabina's father. Other details are lacking. Sr. A. Vincenza writes that he is from the neighbourhood of Gragnano. His wife agreed to receive the girls and the

Sisters for an outing in the country and to put up for a while any girl who needs good air. (Cf. L Rapallino to M. Rosa, 9.9.74).

8 for the M. President: cf. L 38, n. 1.

9 If Mgr Augusto Negrotto (cf. L 71, n. 3) has the school closed, it is well that the President of the St Monica Catholic Circle, Maria Schnaider, should know that it is he who wants it.

10 Cf. L 304,1.

11 To Fr Tornatore.

She speaks of the departure of some Sisters and in particular of Sr. A. Palmira, charged with the office of Superior, whom Vincenza must therefore instruct about certain situations and what she is to do.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I have received all your letters. Listen, I wrote to you last night and this morning here I am writing to you again.2 Listen, you tell me that Sr. A. Battistina has a fever; well then, you can send for Sr. A. Cunegonda, because at S. P. d'Arena they are in extreme need, so Sr. A. Cunegonda can go in place of Sr. A. Battistina,3 and so she can come together with Sr. A. Daria.

2. If Sr. A. Palmira has not yet left, you will write two lines for her in my name, saying that she is their Superior and that they are to obey and respect her.4

3. I would like you to give her the apron with the cord and tassels, and to have her make her vows privately by herself until St Anne's day; thus she will be in step with the others, and next year she will renew them as you do; you can give her the formula, and let her go and make them at the feet of Saint Anne without anyone noticing.5

4. You will tell her that as soon as she arrives she is to go to Trastevere and not to Tor de' Specchi; it is better so; from there they can send someone to fetch her, whereas at Tor de' Specchi they have no one.6

5. Listen, you will tell her that I have written to Tor de' Specchi that when she has arrived, two of them – the first to be the teachers – are to go to the Parrocchietta for 8 or 10 days; then, when these have returned, the other two will go.7

6. Daria will do the cooking, and let her take care to do it well, to satisfy the Sisters with good soup and a good main dish; and those who go to the Parrocchietta will take food with them.

7. Listen, I have thought of sending you four or 6 pieces of preserve, which the Superior gives me, so that you will have that much less to make. Tomorrow I shall also send you the grapes, so that Carlottina may eat a few; they say they are very good.

8. Please God that person went to Cortemaggiore today.8

9. For charity's sake, send Sr. A. Palmira to Rome quickly, for if you knew what is to be found there, it is a horror; tell her also never to allow any little girl to sleep at Tor de' Specchi, but only to be there by day; for sleeping they must all be at Trastevere. I hear they have two there;9 for pity's sake, I hope God will enlighten you to tell her everything properly. Goodbye, your affectionate

M. ROSA

10. Greet Carlotta and all the religious for me, while I implore for them a thousand blessings from heaven; for charity's sake let them pray for what

I wrote to you last night; I am in the greatest distress.10

1 It was catalogued among the letters to an unknown addressee, but it is clearly to Sr. A. Vincenza Rapallino.

2 This is L 309.

3 She has a fever – so Sr. A. Vincenza wrote the previous day – and is in bed. Sr. A. Cunegonda Conti may go in her place.

4 Sr. A. Palmira Grillotti. You will give her two lines in my name presenting her to the community as Superior.

5 I would like... as you do. It is well that she wear the full habit (including the cord with the tassels) and make her vows privately and secretly until St Anne's, so that next year she can renew them together with the other Sisters.

6 You will tell her that from the station she must go to the house in Trastevere, because those Sisters are able to collect her on her arrival.

7 Tell her that the Sisters at Tor de' Specchi have already been told that two at a time, beginning with the teachers, will go to the Parrocchietta for 8 or 10 days, taking their lunch with them each day.

8 That person: Fr Tornatore had already gone there; Sr. A. Vincenza will tell her so on 9.9.

9 Cf. L 309,4.

10 What she wrote about Ricchini, cf. L 309,2.

She encloses two letters to be delivered to their addressees. She approves all that Vincenza has done. She feels their separation perhaps more than Vincenza does. She will write to Carlotta.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. You always owe me letters, so you will not complain; I enclose this letter, which is the bursar's; you will hear what it says, and so it will be of use to you; the other to its destination, that is, you will hand it to him, for I hope he will still be at Piacenza.1

2. For the rest, I hear what you tell me about the Sisters and the accounts; everything is fine and I approve what you have done; I imagine how much work you will have dispatching the Sisters.2

3. Dear Vincenza, this separation certainly seems much longer to me than to you, because when one travels about a great deal..., whereas having to stay always still, writing and talking...;3 now I must go; tomorrow I shall write to Carlotta. Goodbye; greet all the Sisters for me, and believe me eternally

your affectionate M.

1 The bursar's letter: L 314; the other is for Father Tornatore.

2 for dispatching the Sisters who were to leave for Rome.

3 ...than to you, because when one travels about a great deal, one is on the move and has not even time to think and grieve, whereas it is quite another thing when one must stay always still, writing and talking.

She could not answer his letter sooner because she was suffering from severe rheumatism, which still shows no sign of healing. She has received a second letter and assures him that she has never made any personal confidence to Countess Caracciolo, nor could she have acted otherwise. She would like to be converted, but lacks the strength and can do nothing but make a mess of things.

A.M.F.

Good Father Agostino,

1. The reason I was slow to answer yours, which gave me news of your happy journey as soon as you could,2 was that I was seized by severe rheumatism, which took hold of my whole body; for five days now it has settled on my right cheek and gives me spasmodic pains, the whole side swelling up; my teeth, which have tuned up together very nicely, make a marvellous music; my head and my ear are so charming, at certain moments only, that they kindly oblige me to lie down because I faint; but this evening, though bandaged and with this company, I will not go to bed without first writing a couple of ill-strung lines to you, Father Agostino.

2. Today I received your second letter, in which you speak to me of the Countess and of all she said during the evening, and also of the Mother House.3 Listen, Father Agostino – though it seems useless to me to say this to one who ought to know me well enough – I did not make even the least of the least confidences to the dear Countess – how could I, if I have nothing to say? –; these were always my words; if then God told them to her, as she said… but you must tell her that everything she said to me she said to see whether I would agree; but quite the contrary, for I would have to be recast all over again; both in writing and in speaking I never change, I am always the same.4

3. Father Agostino, how can we act otherwise than as we are? Poor Rosa will always be a remnant of the world, and now that, all zeal, she would be for her conversion, she lacks the strength and cannot do as St Augustine did. He was strong, but this corpse can do nothing but make a mess of things.

4. Father Agostino, is it true that they have cholera in Rome? Be cheerful, take courage; the Eternal Father will see to the rest. Believe that he does it gladly; my eyes are closing. If you see the Count, give him my particular regards; I urge him to leave Rome. I am your poorest

Sister ANNA MARIA ROSA GATTORNO

1 The date is deduced from the context.

2 to his of 4 September, from Foligno, where he had gone, leaving from

Piacenza.

3 This second letter of his has not been preserved.

4 From what the Mother says, it can be deduced that Fr Agostino was displeased because she had confided something of her spirit to Countess Isabella Caracciolo,

whereas with him she was always extremely reserved.

She asks her why she is upset at her absence and tries to persuade her to be cheerful, explaining that she is not enjoying herself at all; on the contrary, she is unwell and has a great deal of work at Nizza, and afterwards will go to Acqui and Ovada.

A.M.F.

My dear Carlottina,

1. Why are you so upset with me?1 Remember that I am so busy that I do nothing but write; you think I am enjoying myself with Sr. A. Benedetta, it is not true, she is sad and temptations, troubles; me trouble because I have no head for talking with Sr. A. Benedetta.2

2. I will tell you everything later. You say: “poor me!”; instead you should say: “poor mamma”. Today, as I write to you, I have such a bad headache that even my nerves are curling up, and I am alone; “poor mamma”; you are well and enjoying yourself with Onorata.3

3. Rest assured that there is nothing here to enjoy; I have seen Peppina only once, because she has to work hard, she has the washing, so she told me.4

4. I long for the moment to leave and hope to go to Ovada on Saturday, on Monday at the latest. I am going by way of Acqui, because you know I have to go to the Bishop; and then I shall not come back to Nizza, I shall go straight on by the same road from Acqui to Ovada; you, who have nothing to do or think about, imagine that it is like that.5

1 On 4 September Carlotta had written to her: “I am sorry a little, because not go Nizza, poor alone Carlotta!”.

2 Note how she adapts to her daughter's style and way of expressing herself. Sr. A.

Benedetta Carrega.

3 You say... instead you should say: she directs her to look at, understand and share her mother's life and sufferings, and to value the closeness and friendship of Onorata (Colli), a truly devoted person.

4 Peppina is surely the niece of the Parish Priest Ludovico Bisio, a friend of hers.

5 She tells her about her itinerary and her work, so that she may understand properly and neither suffer nor complain.

She does not object to the Sisters being paid in money rather than in kind, and proposes the corresponding sum. She also suggests the remuneration for the other Sisters who are to be taken on at their request.

Most Honourable Congregation of Charity,

1. I am informed by the Superior there that this Congregation of Charity would like to give in money what it gives in kind, and I willingly agree. I would have wished Your Most Illustrious Lordships to set the price, but since you want it from me, I keep to the bare and economical expense or sum, which is fr. 250.1

2. And for the additional Sisters you wish to have, I intended that they should have at least 150 fr. each; however, I do not wish to displease you in anything; sure of your support, they cannot perish.2

3. I await a line of confirmation, and at the same time notification of when I am to send them.

Believe me, Your Most Illustrious Lordships,

Your most humble Servant, Sister ANNA MARIA ROSA GATTORNO

1 to give in money the payment they now make in kind.

2 For the two additional Sisters (cf. L 175,7), however, I do not wish to displease you in anything. She had insisted and waited so long before they decided to accept them!

(cf. L 245,1).

Two postulants will arrive, one of them without a dowry or the necessities. Vincenza is to provide what is needed for now and prepare a curtained bed for them. She is sending things for Carlotta and for Vincenza. She urges her to write and to take care of herself. The sorrows are many, but may God's will be done with love and generosity. It is wise to provide for the winter, so she should buy maize, asking the Father for the money.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Today I do not even have letters from you; I hope nothing is wrong. I am taking advantage of the departure of these two postulants, who are truly very good and dear; one is strong and can also help with the washing, the other too, but I would very much like you to see that this one, whose name is Luigia, stays, as I hope she will; listen, I am sending you enclosed a list which belongs to this blessed girl.1

2. Listen, go to Poss and collect all the things you see listed here, and then send them on; patience is needed; only the stockings are very old, and so are the handkerchiefs and the foot-coverlet and everything, the old little dress; it is unbelievable; with these people one must arm oneself with great patience!2

3. Listen, this postulant Luigia, owing to a very curious circumstance, has brought nothing, not even s...; try to give her a few; listen, in the drawer of the chest of the little Infant there are some, and you can give her those, which are Sr. A. Augusta's; and you can give her two of the shirts they have made; for now give her only a little to change into, yes, and assign her a pigeonhole now, and they will give her everything she needs, as they do the nuns; her place; better still, if there were a bed with curtains it would be good, for she will be better off there, with no nuns about; and you can put one in the big dormitory, so that she is apart from the religious; I hope you have understood me.3

4. I shall not leave Nizza until next Monday the 14th, and I go to Acqui and, on the same side, without coming back here to Nizza, to Ovada, where I shall stay only 6 or 7 days, for your guidance.4 If Carlotta is still at Piacenza, tell her to give one of her used hats to Onorata, and you too have it done up for her, because it would look better. Tell her that today I sent the chickens for her to the nuns; to you I am sending three turkeys and a little basket of grapes for you; keep them for yourself. The Superior is sending you the preserve; this note from Sr. A. Benedetta, if Carlottina is not there, burn it, that is better.

5. I gather you are all in ecstasy, since you no longer write; I have had no letters from you since Sunday; pray, for I am forced to write to you, otherwise I would like to pay you back in the same coin; today I wrote 10 letters, and yet this evening I am writing to you too, enough; listen, do not wear yourself out; do you know what I fear? that you will do more than your strength allows and then fall ill; for charity's sake take care of yourself, do not get up if you do not feel well, because it could do you harm; in the evening go to bed early, so as to regain your strength.5

6. Tell the one at Poss that when relatives go there, or anyone at all, she is not to let them go into the girls' refectory, because she let a woman from Nizza go there, and so she told everything she saw.6 It seems impossible that they let people go everywhere; have they no parlour for receiving visitors? So one must go through every kind of thing; because there are not enough of them already, it is like a storm with hail a kilo to the hailstone; enough.7

7. May God's will be done in all things; ah, yes, my daughter, may it be that which consumes us and destroys us; be sure that if the good God now makes us suffer horribly, a day will also come when everything will be over, and we shall have what we so desire.8

8. I urge you to receive well that person whom you will have seen; Father Mancini recommends her to us. Write me something about whether you will hold the clothing after the Retreat; then Father Mancini will sleep in the Father's room, and so the guest quarters will not get so worn.9

9. Dear Vincenza, how many sorrows, how many tribulations, but everything for dear Jesus is always little; He alone and for Him alone; that is enough for everything.10

10. It would be good for you to lay in a little store of maize; tell that person to buy it with the money left over to him, which he has received; he can buy plenty of maize for this winter; have it put in the grain room; he can have it bought from our miller, who I see is better than the others; think also of having a little fodder or maize leavings bought for the pigs; it is true that for now it is better to keep them on bran, so that they grow and do not fatten. Goodbye, I am tired, it is late, your affectionate M., eternally yours, [M. ROSA]

1 The two postulants: Luisola Luigia and a certain Annunciata (Reg. Post.

266, 267). The enclosed list is Luisola's; to be precise, it is the list of the personal belongings of her sister Giuseppina, who, as appears from the pay sheets for April 1874, had been taken on as a worker in the Poss factory

(cf. AFSA, FPof). Having left suddenly with the father of another girl who had come to fetch his daughter, she had left her things behind.

2 The Mother charges Sr. A. Vincenza with collecting the things, according to the list. Old things, but they want them.

3 To this postulant, owing to a curious, strange circumstance, perhaps a misunderstanding or the Parish Priest's advice, her relatives have brought nothing, not even stockings; try to give her the small outfit that may be of use to her... assign her the pigeon-hole, that is, the place in the wardrobe room, her place (bando) in the dormitory.

4 Cf. L 305,6; 307,3; 313,4.

5 do not wear yourself out... take care of yourself. Sr. A. Vincenza in her letters gave her precise accounts of how the two houses were going, to which had been added the considerable work of the Poss factory. And M. Rosa was well aware of the overwork and sacrifices all this entailed for her daughter, whose health was so delicate.

6 The one at Poss: Sr. A. Valentina Giorgi, the person in charge.

7 a kilo to the hailstone: to each grain.

8 the good God makes us suffer horribly, permits us to live through tragic situations, but these will end and He will make us share in the joy we desire (cf. Heb 12:5-7).

9 Father Alessandro Mancini SJ held M. Rosa and her Institute in high esteem and sent several postulants there.

10 The love that makes her welcome tribulations with her gaze turned to Jesus gives her the measure of His Love, a LOVE that absorbs and transcends our littleness.

11 As a good and provident mother of a family, she concerns herself with provisions for the winter; tell Father Tornatore to give you the money left over and buy maize for the whole winter... and fodder.

1 9

She has received her letter and is pleased with what she wrote about the Hospital. She knows nothing of Carlotta and Onorata's departure for Genoa. She is not writing at length because they will soon see each other: in a few days she leaves for Ovada and will then be in Genoa.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I have received your letter. I am glad to hear what you tell me about the Hospital; your little crosses, which are made of sugar.1

2. You speak of a newspaper, but I have not seen anything yet; I hope you will send it to me if it comes out.2 Listen, on Monday, God willing, I leave for Ovada, going by way of Acqui; in the evening I shall be at Ovada, for your guidance, but I think I shall stay there only three or four days, because then I want to come to Genoa.3 Today Carlottina was to leave Piacenza together with Onorata; so far I know nothing.

3. As for the visits those doctors are making to the hospital, there must certainly be something behind it; we shall see; enough, let us leave everything to the Lord, for he will always do what is best for us.4

4. Do not complain that I write little to you, because, dear daughter, we shall tell each other everything in person; because it pains me to write so much.5 So if you have anything urgent, write to me; otherwise we shall see each other, God willing, next week. If you have the newspaper, send it to me.

Goodbye, your

affectionate M.

I hope you have taken Sr. A. Battistina in with you.6

1 The letter is dated the 6th of this month. The little sugar crosses: a disagreement with the

Director of the Hospital, a Sister or two in bed.

2 you speak of a newspaper: “during the week a newspaper is to come out (concerning the hospital) and if there is anything in our favour I will send it to you”, Francesca had written to her.

3 Cf. L 315, n. 4.

4 Several distinguished persons had visited the hospital and had greatly praised its order and cleanliness.

5 The Mother suffered greatly when she wrote at length, because of the stigmata she bore in her hands. Cf. Fisionomia Spirituale, p. 121.

6 Cf. L 305, n. 1.

Her sheet full of holy resolutions has awakened in the Mother signs of grace and faithfulness to God's Work. She entrusts her to Mary and to Saint Anne, and prays to the Eternal Father together with her dear daughter, promising him love and faithfulness.

1. My daughter, your sheet, full of such holy resolutions, has awakened in me signs of grace and of perseverance and faithfulness to God's Work in you!2 May Most Holy Mary, with her victorious heel, seal your promises and never again allow that any diabolical assault, whether through affection, or human respect, or to please this vile body, may ever be the reason for this seal to be lifted; on the contrary. O you, my beloved mother Saint Anne, with your strong arm do not allow any of these things to come near to move it.3

2. Eternal Father, your servant offers you her blood in faithfulness to all she promises you. Enlighten me by sending me your Spirit; strengthen me by giving me your love, your most beloved Son; defend me with your most mighty arm; and before the heavenly Court I promise you love and faithfulness. May I be yours for ever.4

Affectionately, MOTHER ROSA. You will always be dear to me. May Jesus be always with you.5

1 No place is given, since the addressee was at Nizza with the Mother.

2 She had welcomed her daughter into the Institute as an outstanding gift of God for

His Work and was forming her by keeping her close. But one day the storm of temptation came and the young woman had drawn away from her. “She is sad and temptations, troubles; me trouble because I have no head for talking”, so M. Rosa wrote to Carlotta (L 313,1). Then Benedetta had understood, come to her senses and written her a sheet full of holy resolutions. The Mother, who had seen the hopes placed in her waver, sees again the signs of her vocation and of a persevering and faithful response.

3 She entrusts her promises to Mary and asks her for victory over every form of temptation. She asks Saint Anne to protect her with her strong arm.

4 She concludes with the beautiful trinitarian prayer. A spiritual outpouring of the Mother for the one she has begotten as a daughter, a gift the daughter receives as a pledge of strength, in her commitment of love and faithfulness to Jesus.

5 Always: it is the seal of a tenderness that transcends time and is centred in Jesus.

She advises her about the economy of the House. She asks for vests for herself and Sr. A. Benedetta because it is cold; if they are sent by Sunday they will receive them, since they leave on Monday. Fr Milano has asked her to have stockings made for a merchant. If the cotton arrives, Vincenza will know what it is for.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. Last night I received your long letter.1 First of all, I would like you to stop making bread and keep the grain for the winter; at least do not make it for the girls, and keep the second-grade flour for this winter; you may make it for yourselves, but if you give it to the girls, in two days there will be none left. It is best for you to mix all the second-grade flour.

2. I hear about the one from Cortemaggiore; if she is not willing to stay, let her go, it matters little; from now on we must be begged, not do the begging.2

3. I commend the grain to you, for charity's sake; if any money comes to you, buy more, and maize as well. Remember to have the mason give you his account, so that it can be paid off little by little: now 200, now 100; in the end [the debt] is cleared; I long for it. You know how much debts hurt me. I would really like to begin 1875 without debts; I hope to.

4. It is very cold here, and neither I nor Sr. A. Benedetta brought a vest; if you receive this early you could send us some. She would like cotton ones,

which she has in her pigeon-hole, and I woollen ones. If they arrived on Sunday they would still be in time.

5. For charity's sake, tell me something about the postulants, for I am anxious. You tell me you get no sweeties from anyone; I do not believe it, because I know it is otherwise. Enough, I do not want to say everything.4

6. What is Poss doing? Is it true that he is building the privy and all the other things he promised? Then we shall start bringing in girls; you can write so to the man at Soresina who had so many. What does Liberati say, is she becoming a nun or not? Has she answered the Father?... Write me something.

7. At last on Monday I shall be at Ovada, in the evening. I am not writing to Carlotta because I think she will already have left.6 Here Fr Milano wanted me to take on some stockings, but he will send you the cotton; the cost of sending it, and yours of sending back the finished stockings, is borne by him, the merchant.7 Only it is little: (only) 30 cent. The Superior tells me it is little; they are short socks; what do they give you there? The sample, as you will see, is close-knit, but he wants them looser. Meanwhile I have already told him it is little, and he will be written to that he must give more. So if you receive cotton you will know what to do. I forgot to send you the stockings I have as a sample. Goodbye, yours for ever and ever,

your affectionate MOTHER

1 It is dated 9 September. Sr. A. Vincenza had written to her: “we have begun to make bread at home and it turns out nicely”, and proposed sending the second-grade flour to the girls working at the Poss factory. The Mother is of a different opinion.

2 the one from Cortemaggiore, a postulant “always undecided about taking the habit, yes and no, she lacks the eagerness of the others, sometimes she cries... I encourage her”, writes Vincenza.

3 Without debts. It is a wish she has never seen fulfilled so far.

4 You tell me: here are the exact words she uses to her jokingly, adopting

Carlotta's style: “poor me, alone, abandoned by all. Yesterday angry with that

Person (Fr Tornatore) because stingy, consolations never! The Mother neither sends me any” (ibid.).

5 The Mother had asked him for sanitary facilities and other work in the girls' section. Cf. L 280,1. The man at Soresina: the Vicar, Fr Luigi Malfina, to send girls to work. Carolina Liberati, a lady from Rome who wanted to enter the Institute with her two daughters (cf. Sr. A. Eletta Bruschi to M. Rosa, 27.6.74).

6 Carlotta was to go to Genoa.

7 Fr Luigi Milano wanted me to accept some work: making stockings for a merchant he knows; he will send the cotton and the money for sending the stockings back to the merchant.

She has received the accounts and is very glad to see that only 100 fr. of debt remain. She encloses the draft of a letter informing the Countess of a girl's dismissal. Exhortations to prudence and faithfulness to the Lord.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I have received your letter with the account inside; what you have done is fine, that is enough. I am glad to see that you have no more than F. 100 of debt, a small matter, which with one more month will be entirely paid off.

2. My dear daughter, listen, you tell me to send Pulga away; do so, and I am sending you a letter to copy and send to the Countess, thanking her for what she sent you; you will read it; and so you will also tell her to send away this insolent girl, who is a scandal to the others, now that other little girls are beginning to come.1

3. My dear, do not think I am sending you this copy because I think you are not capable, no, quite the contrary; it is only so that you can see how it should be framed, since I cannot explain it to you properly for lack of time.2 It is true that I shall have to leave Rosa and the other one; what can I do, my dear, the Countess does not want me to remove them, so I was able to promise her not to remove them; patience is needed. For charity's sake, say nothing of this, lest the two come to know (it); so be of good heart.3

4. Listen, when that person you know of comes to bring you messages,4 be sparing in your answers; and when she talks to you about money, never complain, do not tell her you have debts; but if she should tell you that this and that must be done, answer her: “My lady, I can do nothing more than what my Superiors order me; what would you have, we are daughters of obedience; write it to the mother and she will tell me what I must do”, and cut it short, for charity's sake.

5. Ah, blessed the moment when you tell me: “everything is paid and I have a little left over in reserve”; I wish it for you with all my soul.5 Courage, forward, daughter, for Jesus is pleased; try to be faithful to him and you will have everything. Goodbye, your affectionate M.

Greet everyone for me; God bless you.

On Monday I leave for Ovada;6 send my letters to Genoa, where I shall be shortly.

1 About the girl Matilde Pulga: “I would like you to give me permission to send her away, for she is the ruin of all the others”, so the Superior. The Mother consents. She sends her the outline of the letter she is to write to Countess Trotti.

2 She explains why she sent her the copy, fearing that the Sister might take offence.

3 It is true that she is not transferring Sr. A. Rosa (cf. L 295,2); she explains why.

4 That person: Signora Teresina Zagatti, the countess's secretary.

5 Cf. L 318, n. 3.

6 Monday, 13 September.

She writes from Invorio Inferiore, where she is to establish a community; Vincenza should therefore send Sisters Paola and Gesuina. She asks her to send a copy of the permissions granted for the Institute's Chapels.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. Since last night I have been in this village on Lake Maggiore. You will have received my telegram, and I am awaiting the religious, two: Paola and Gesuina, because I shall take the others from other places.1 You will have been anxious at having no letters from me.

2. After a very odd and quite exhausting journey we reached our destination last night at 9[½]; this village is called Invorio Inferiore; it is two hours by carriage, but we took four, because we went to the Vicar; today I shall do another two hours to go to the Bishop, Mgr Gentile.2

3. Listen, send me the papers at once, that is, the copy of the permission for the Chapels; copy all the permissions we have and send them to this address: Boffetti Giovanni, Parish Priest of Vespolate.3

4. We are [at] Invorio Inferiore; do not write to me, because I hope to leave on Friday and go to Ovada, where I shall arrive at night.4 Oh, where are we, my God! Tell that person not to write to me until he has letters from me, to stay put. Goodbye. Will Carlotta have left? It seems a hundred

I am at the end of the world, yours in haste

years since I saw her

Affectionately, M. R.

1 Sr. A. Paola Bucciotti and Sr. A. Gesuina Moroni.

2 Mgr Giacomo Gentile, Bishop of Novara.

3 The permissions, that is, the faculties granted by Pius IX on 24 January 1866. (Cf.

L 160). The Parish Priest of Vespolate (Prov. of Novara) is Fr Giovanni Boffetti. Cf.

L 388, n. 3.

4 Friday the 17th.

5 Will she have gone to Genoa? (cf. L 315,4; 318,7).
